title: Albert Bandura: Modeling Theory
overview: Albert Bandura agreed with Skinner that behavior is learned, but argued that people learn most of what they do by watching others in a social setting, not only through direct reinforcement. His social-learning (observational-learning) theory centres on vicarious reinforcement and on cognitive processes that sit between stimulus and response, making it a milder form of behaviorism. Through the Bobo doll studies he showed how children copy aggressive models, and he described disinhibition and the model, observer and reward factors that shape imitation. Observational learning runs through four processes: attention, retention, production and motivation. The self, for Bandura, is a set of cognitive processes; its two key aspects are self-reinforcement and self-efficacy, the belief that one can cope and control life events, which is built from performance attainment, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion and physiological arousal and which changes across the life span. Bandura applied modeling, guided participation and covert modeling to fears, phobias and anxiety, defended behavior modification against ethical charges, and described behavior through reciprocal determinism. The chapter reviews extensive research on self-efficacy, collective efficacy, Internet self-efficacy and the link between media violence and aggression, and ends with criticisms and the worldwide use of role models.
objectives: Explain how Bandura's social-learning approach differs from Skinner's behaviorism, including vicarious reinforcement and the mediating role of cognitive processes.
Describe the Bobo doll studies and other modeling research, and explain disinhibition, including online trolling.
Discuss how the characteristics of models, the characteristics of observers and reward consequences influence modeling.
Explain the four processes of observational learning (attentional, retention, production, incentive and motivational) and how they are related.
Define self-reinforcement and self-efficacy, describe high and low self-efficacy, the four sources of efficacy information and ways of increasing self-efficacy.
Trace the development of self-efficacy from infancy to old age.
Describe modeling, guided participation and covert modeling as behavior-modification techniques, their uses for fears, phobias and anxiety, their advantages and the ethical issues raised.
State Bandura's position on human nature (reciprocal determinism), his assessment methods and research style.
Summarise research on self-efficacy, collective efficacy, Internet self-efficacy and the effects of televised, online and video-game violence on aggression.
Evaluate the criticisms and contributions of Bandura's theory, including the global use of role models.

sections.heading: The Social-Learning Approach and Vicarious Reinforcement
sections.detailed:
Bandura shared one basic belief with Skinner: behavior is learned. Beyond that, the two parted ways. Bandura objected to Skinner's reliance on single animal subjects, arguing that findings from experiments with no social interaction cannot be expected to tell us much about real life, since hardly anyone lives in social isolation. His alternative is a social-learning theory, which studies how behavior is formed and changed within a social context, among human beings interacting with each other.

Vicarious reinforcement. Bandura accepted that a great deal of learning comes from reinforcement, but he insisted that almost every kind of behavior can also be learned without the learner ever being reinforced directly. For this reason his approach is also called observational learning, which the chapter defines as acquiring new responses by watching how other people behave. Instead of having to be rewarded for every action ourselves, we watch others act and notice what happens to them as a result. Learning or strengthening a behavior in this way, through the consequences experienced by someone else, is vicarious reinforcement.

This emphasis on learning by example rather than always by direct reinforcement is the most distinctive feature of Bandura's theory. It explains how we can pick up behaviors we have never been rewarded for, and how we can avoid behaviors we have seen others punished for, without going through those consequences personally.

For exams, note the contrast clearly: Skinner said behavior is shaped by the consequences that follow one's own responses; Bandura said behavior is also shaped by the consequences we observe in others, and that this social, observational route accounts for most human learning.
sections.simple: Bandura agreed with Skinner that behavior is learned, but said we mostly learn it by watching other people. We see what happens to them when they act and then copy or avoid that behavior. This learning through someone else's rewards and punishments is called vicarious reinforcement, and it is the heart of his theory.
keyPoints: Agreed with Skinner that behavior is learned; criticised his focus on single animal subjects.
Social-learning theory studies behavior as it is formed and changed in a social context.
Also called observational learning: learning new responses by watching others.
Vicarious reinforcement: learning from the consequences others receive, not one's own.
Learning by example rather than only by direct reinforcement is Bandura's distinctive idea.

sections.heading: The Role of Cognitive Processes and A Less Extreme Form of Behaviorism
sections.detailed:
The role of cognitive processes. A second feature that separates Bandura from Skinner is his acceptance of internal thought processes. Skinner refused to bring cognition into his explanations; Bandura argued that cognitive processes shape observational learning. We do not copy everything we see in a mechanical way. Instead, we make a deliberate and conscious decision to act as the model did. To learn from example and from vicarious reinforcement, we must be able to anticipate the consequences of the behaviors we watch and appreciate what they would mean for us.

Because we can picture or imagine these consequences, we can regulate and steer our own behavior even though we have never experienced those outcomes ourselves. Skinner proposed a direct link between stimulus and response, or between behavior and reinforcer. Bandura rejected this: in his view, there is no direct link, because cognitive processes mediate between the two. What we think about a situation and its likely consequences sits between what happens to us and what we do.

A less extreme form of behaviorism. Taken together, these points make Bandura's theory a milder version of behaviorism than Skinner's. He kept the behaviorist focus on learning but added two things: learning by observing others, and the mediating role of cognition. His work also rests on a different kind of evidence. It is built on rigorous laboratory research with normal people interacting socially, rather than on a rat in a cage (Skinner) or a neurotic patient on a couch (psychoanalysis).

This section answers a common review question about how Bandura handles internal cognitive processes: he accepts them as mediators that let us anticipate consequences, decide whether to imitate, and regulate our own behavior, while still studying them through controlled experiments.
sections.simple: Unlike Skinner, Bandura believed our thoughts matter. We don't copy behavior automatically; we think about what will happen and then decide whether to imitate. So thinking sits between the stimulus and our response. That makes his theory a softer kind of behaviorism, tested with normal people in social situations.
keyPoints: Cognitive processes influence observational learning; imitation is a conscious decision.
We must anticipate and appreciate the consequences of observed behavior.
No direct stimulus-response link: cognition mediates between them.
Less extreme behaviorism: adds observation and cognition to learning.
Based on lab research with normal people in social interaction, not rats or neurotic patients.

sections.heading: The Life of Bandura (1925–)
sections.detailed:
Get drunk or go to school. Bandura was born in Alberta, Canada, in a town so small that its high school had just two teachers and 20 students. His parents were immigrants from Poland who valued education. His mother put the choice bluntly: he could work in the fields and end up drinking in the beer parlor, or he could get an education. He chose education.

In the summer after finishing high school he worked on a construction crew in the Yukon wilderness, filling holes in the Alaska Highway. Many of his co-workers were people running away from creditors, alimony and probation officers. Bandura later said this odd group gave him a sharp appreciation of the psychopathology of everyday life.

Finding psychology. He studied as an undergraduate at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver and took psychology purely for convenience. He commuted in a carpool with engineering and pre-med students who all had early classes, and a psychology course happened to be offered at that hour. He soon found the subject fascinating and went on to a Ph.D. from the University of Iowa in 1952.

After a year at the Wichita, Kansas, Guidance Center, he joined Stanford University, where he developed his new approach. Challenging Skinner's behaviorism, then the dominant position, was risky for a young unknown psychologist; Bandura later described behaviorism as having had a stranglehold on psychology when he began his research on observational learning.

He nonetheless became very successful and published widely. In 1973, just 21 years after his doctorate, he was elected president of the American Psychological Association. He received the APA's Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award in 1980 and the American Psychological Foundation's Gold Medal Award for Life Achievement in 2006. He was also known for humor directed at himself: asked whether he walked or drove to his office, he said both, sometimes on the same day, because he would drive in, get lost in thought and absentmindedly walk home, leaving the car behind.
sections.simple: Bandura grew up in a tiny town in Alberta, Canada, with Polish immigrant parents who pushed education. He found psychology by accident because a course fit his carpool timing, then earned a Ph.D. at Iowa in 1952 and worked at Stanford. He challenged Skinner's behaviorism and became APA president in 1973.
keyPoints: Born 1925 in a tiny town in Alberta, Canada, to Polish immigrant parents who valued education.
Summer job on the Alaska Highway taught him about the psychopathology of everyday life.
Took psychology at the University of British Columbia because it fit his carpool schedule.
Ph.D. University of Iowa 1952; Wichita Guidance Center; then Stanford University.
APA president 1973; Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award 1980; APF Gold Medal 2006.

sections.heading: Modeling: The Basis of Observational Learning (Bobo Doll and Other Modeling Studies)
sections.detailed:
Bandura's core idea is that learning can happen through observation or example, not only through direct reinforcement. He did not deny that direct reinforcement influences behavior; what he challenged was the claim that behavior can be learned or changed only that way. He pointed out that operant conditioning, where trial-and-error behavior continues until the correct response happens to occur, is inefficient and can be dangerous for skills such as swimming or driving. A learner might drown or crash before stumbling on the right sequence of actions. For Bandura, most human behavior is learned through example, sometimes intentionally and sometimes accidentally, by watching others and patterning our behavior on theirs.

Modeling means observing a model's behavior and repeating it ourselves. Through modeling we can acquire responses we have never shown before and can also strengthen or weaken responses we already have. (In the margin glossary, modeling is also defined as a behavior-modification technique in which a person observes models and participates with them in performing the desired behavior.)

Bobo the inflatable doll. Bandura's classic demonstration (Bandura, Ross, & Ross, 1963) used Bobo, an inflatable plastic figure about 4 feet tall. Preschool children watched an adult hit and kick the doll while shouting phrases such as telling others to sock him in the nose. When the children were later left alone with Bobo, they copied what they had seen. Compared with a control group who had not seen the model, the experimental group was twice as aggressive. The intensity of aggression was the same whether the model was seen live, on television or as a cartoon character; in all three media the model drew out aggression that the control children did not show to the same degree.

Other modeling studies. Bandura and Walters (1963) compared the parents of highly aggressive children with the parents of inhibited children. As the theory predicted, inhibited children had inhibited parents and aggressive children had aggressive parents; the children had modeled their parents' behavior.

Verbal modeling can also produce behavior, provided the activities are fully and clearly explained. It is often used to give instructions, for example in teaching someone to drive. Verbal instructions are usually combined with behavioral demonstration, as when a driving instructor acts as a model and performs the driving behaviors.
sections.simple: Bandura said most behavior is learned by watching others, which is safer and faster than trial and error. In the Bobo doll study, kids who watched an adult beat up an inflatable doll were twice as aggressive as kids who didn't, whether the model was live, on TV or a cartoon. Children also copy their parents, and spoken instructions can work as a model too.
keyPoints: Learning occurs through observation, not only direct reinforcement; trial and error can be inefficient and dangerous.
Modeling can create new responses and strengthen or weaken existing ones.
Bobo doll (Bandura, Ross, & Ross, 1963): observers were twice as aggressive as controls.
Same intensity of aggression for live, televised and cartoon models.
Bandura & Walters (1963): aggressive and inhibited children had parents like them.
Verbal modeling works if activities are fully explained, usually alongside demonstration.

sections.heading: Disinhibition
sections.detailed:
Research shows that behaviors people usually suppress can be performed more readily when a model is present (Bandura, 1973, 1986). This is disinhibition: the weakening of an inhibition or restraint through exposure to a model. A crowd can turn into a riot, with people breaking windows and shouting, doing things they would never do alone. Seeing others around them act aggressively makes them more likely to drop their own restraints against aggression.

Sexual behavior. Walters, Bowen and Parke (1963) showed that sexual responses can be disinhibited by a model. Male undergraduates watched a film containing erotic pictures of nude men and women. They were told that a moving spot of light showed the eye movements of a previous subject, revealing where that person had looked. This supposed previous subject served as the model. For half the participants the light focused on breasts and genitals; for the other half it stayed on the background, as though the model avoided looking at the bodies. Afterwards, the students viewed stills from the film while their own eye movements were recorded. Those with the uninhibited model looked at the erotic parts of the bodies in the same way; those whose model had avoided the nudes spent significantly more time looking at the background. The researchers concluded that modeling affected perceptual responses: it shaped not only what the participants did but also what they looked at and perceived.

Trolling. Posting comments online after the example of others gives the same anonymity as being in a large crowd. This can produce an online form of disinhibition called trolling, the posting of inflammatory, derogatory or hateful messages about a person or group. Some adolescents have been driven to suicide by cruel, widespread comments directed at them by name (Zhuo, 2010). Among frequent video gamers, those most involved in trolling were younger and male; their reasons ranged from deliberate revenge to boredom to simple amusement (Thacker & Griffiths, 2012).

Decline with age. Disinhibition appears to weaken as people get older. Among Americans aged 18 to 25, disinhibition was strong in 18- to 19-year-olds but much reduced in 22- to 25-year-olds (Vaidya, Latzman, Markon, & Watson, 2010).

The link between mob behavior and trolling, asked in the review questions, is that in both cases the presence of models plus anonymity weakens normal restraints, so people do what they would not do alone.
sections.simple: Disinhibition means seeing a model do something makes us drop our usual self-control. That is why people in a mob riot, and why anonymous people online pile on with hateful comments (trolling). Models even change what we look at, and the effect gets weaker as we move through our twenties.
keyPoints: Disinhibition: weakening of inhibitions by observing a model.
Mobs: people act aggressively when they see others around them doing so.
Walters, Bowen & Parke (1963): a model's 'eye movements' shaped what students looked at in erotic stills.
Trolling is online disinhibition, aided by crowd-like anonymity (Zhuo, 2010).
Trollers among gamers: younger, male; motives were revenge, boredom, amusement (Thacker & Griffiths, 2012).
Disinhibition declines with age: strong at 18-19, much less at 22-25 (Vaidya et al., 2010).

sections.heading: The Effects of Society's Models
sections.detailed:
From his extensive research, Bandura concluded that much of our behavior, good and bad, normal and abnormal, is learned by imitating other people. From infancy we develop responses to the models our society provides. Parents are the first models: from them we learn language and become socialized into the customs and acceptable behaviors of our culture.

People who deviate from cultural norms learned their behavior in exactly the same way as everyone else. The only difference is that they followed models that the rest of society considers undesirable. Abnormal behavior, in other words, is not produced by a different mechanism; it is produced by the same process of modeling applied to the wrong models.

Bad models. Bandura openly criticised societies that provide the wrong models for their children, especially the violent behavior that is routine fare on television, in movies and in video games. His research clearly shows that models affect behavior. If we become what we see, then the gap between watching an aggressive animated character and committing a violent act ourselves is not large.

Modeling also passes on non-rational fears. A child who sees parents become frightened during thunderstorms or nervous around strangers easily takes on these anxieties and carries them into adulthood, usually without knowing where they came from. Equally, positive qualities such as strength, courage and optimism are learned from parents and other models.

The chapter sums up the contrast: in Skinner's system reinforcers control behavior; for Bandura, it is the models who control behavior.
sections.simple: Bandura believed we learn almost everything, good or bad, by copying society's models, starting with our parents. People who behave abnormally simply copied the wrong models. Violent TV, movies and games are bad models, and kids can even pick up irrational fears from their parents. For Skinner reinforcers control behavior; for Bandura models do.
keyPoints: Most behavior, normal and abnormal, is learned by imitating others.
Parents are first models: language, customs and acceptable behaviors.
Deviant people learned the same way but followed undesirable models.
Bandura criticised violent models in TV, movies and video games.
Children pick up non-rational fears (and positive traits) from parents.
Skinner: reinforcers control behavior; Bandura: models control behavior.

sections.heading: Characteristics of the Modeling Situation: The Models
sections.detailed:
Bandura and his associates (Bandura, 1977, 1986) identified three factors that influence modeling: the characteristics of the models, the characteristics of the observers, and the reward consequences linked to the behaviors. This section covers the first.

Models who are like us. We are more influenced by someone who seems similar to us than by someone who differs in obvious and important ways. In the laboratory, children imitated a child model in the same room, a child in a film and a filmed cartoon character, but the amount of imitation fell as similarity between model and child fell. Children copied a live model more than an animated character, though even the cartoon produced significantly more imitation than in a control group that saw no model.

Age and sex of models. We are more likely to model ourselves on someone of the same sex and of our own age. Peers who seem to have successfully solved problems we are now facing are especially influential.

Status of models. Status and prestige matter. Pedestrians are much more likely to cross against a red light when they see a well-dressed person doing so than a poorly dressed one. Television commercials exploit this by having high-status athletes and celebrities endorse products, expecting consumers to imitate them and buy.

Type of behavior displayed. Highly complex behaviors are not imitated as quickly or easily as simple ones. Hostile and aggressive behaviors tend to be strongly imitated, particularly by children. In one study, infants as young as 16 months imitated a model using a tool, a rake to retrieve an out-of-reach toy, but only if they had first been shown the object or purpose of using the tool (Esseilly, Rat-Fischer, O'Regan, & Fagard, 2013). American college students who had observed a positive caregiver-child relationship successfully modeled that behavior in their own romantic relationships (Kuhn & Kinsky, 2013).

Size and weight of models. A study of 9th- and 10th-grade students in Canada found that those attending schools where older students tended to be overweight or obese gained more weight than students at schools where older students were not overweight (Leatherdale & Papadakis, 2011).
sections.simple: Three things affect modeling: the model, the observer and the rewards. We copy models who are similar to us, the same sex and age, high in status, and showing simple or aggressive behavior. Even a model's weight can rub off, as students at schools with overweight seniors gained more weight.
keyPoints: Three factors: model characteristics, observer characteristics, reward consequences (Bandura, 1977, 1986).
Similar models are imitated more; live more than cartoon, but cartoons still beat no model.
Same-sex, same-age and successful peer models are more influential.
High-status models are copied more (red-light crossing; celebrity ads).
Simple and aggressive behaviors are imitated more readily than complex ones.
Studies: infants and tools (Esseilly et al., 2013); romantic relationships (Kuhn & Kinsky, 2013); weight (Leatherdale & Papadakis, 2011).

sections.heading: Characteristics of the Modeling Situation: The Observers and Reward Consequences
sections.detailed:
Age of observers. In infancy, modeling is limited to immediate imitation. Infants have not yet developed the cognitive capacities, the imaginal and verbal representational systems, needed to imitate a behavior some time after seeing it. For infants, the modeled behavior has to be repeated several times after the infant first tries to copy it, and it must fall within the infant's range of sensorimotor development. By about age 2, children have developed enough attentional, retention and production ability to imitate behavior some time after observing it rather than only immediately.

The kind of reinforcement we respond to, and therefore what we choose to imitate, changes with age. Younger children are reinforced mainly by physical stimuli such as food, affection or punishment. Older children link positive physical reinforcers with signs of approval from significant models, and unpleasant ones with signs of disapproval. Eventually these rewards and punishments become self-administered. This sequence answers the review question on how the behaviors we acquire through modeling change with age.

Attributes of the observers. People low in self-confidence and self-esteem are much more likely to imitate a model than people high in these qualities. A person who has been reinforced for imitating, for example a child praised for acting like an older sibling, is more susceptible to models than a child who has not been reinforced in this way.

Reward consequences. The rewards linked to a behavior can affect how much modeling occurs and can even override the effects of model and observer characteristics. A high-status model may lead us to copy a behavior, but if the rewards are not meaningful to us we will stop the behavior and be less influenced by that model in future.

Seeing a model rewarded or punished also affects imitation. In a Bobo doll study (Bandura, 1965), one group of children saw the model who hit Bobo receive praise, soda and candy; another group saw the model verbally and physically punished for the same aggression. The children who saw the punishment were significantly less aggressive toward the doll than those who saw the model reinforced.
sections.simple: Babies can only copy right away; by about age 2 children can copy later from memory. Young kids respond to physical rewards, older kids to approval, and eventually people reward themselves. Low self-esteem people copy more, and seeing a model rewarded makes us copy more while seeing them punished makes us copy less.
keyPoints: Infants imitate only immediately; they lack imaginal and verbal representational systems.
By about age 2, delayed imitation becomes possible.
Reinforcers shift with age: physical stimuli, then approval/disapproval, then self-administered.
Low self-confidence/self-esteem and past reinforcement for imitating increase modeling.
Reward consequences can override model and observer characteristics.
Bandura (1965): seeing the model punished reduced children's aggression toward Bobo.

sections.heading: The Processes of Observational Learning: Attentional Processes
sections.detailed:
Bandura analysed observational learning and concluded that it is governed by four related mechanisms: attentional processes, retention processes, production processes, and incentive and motivational processes (Table 13.1). They are related because each depends on the others: we cannot remember what we did not attend to, cannot produce what we did not retain, and motivation affects how much we attend to and retain in the first place.

Attentional processes come first. Modeling will not occur unless the observer pays attention to the model. Simply being exposed to a model does not guarantee that a person will notice the relevant cues and events or even perceive the situation accurately. The observer must perceive the model accurately enough to acquire the information needed to imitate the behavior. Table 13.1 describes this as developing our cognitive and perceptual skills so we can attend to a model and perceive it accurately; its example is staying awake in driver's education class.

Several variables influence attention. In real life as in the laboratory, we attend more to some people and situations than to others, and the more closely we attend, the more likely we are to imitate. Model characteristics already discussed, such as age, status, sex and similarity, help determine how closely we attend. Celebrity models, experts, and models who appear confident and attractive command more attention and imitation than those who lack these attributes. Some of the most effective models in American culture today appear on television, YouTube and other online sites, and viewers often focus on them even when there is no reinforcement.

Attention also depends on the observer's cognitive and perceptual skills and on the value of the behavior. The more developed our cognitive abilities and the more we know about the behavior being modeled, the more carefully we attend and perceive it. We pay more attention when we expect to perform the behavior ourselves than when it has no personal relevance, and more attention to behavior that produces positive or negative consequences than to behavior with neutral outcomes.
sections.simple: Observational learning has four linked steps: attention, retention, production and motivation. The first is paying attention, because you can't copy what you didn't notice properly. We attend more to similar, high-status, expert, confident or attractive models, to behavior we expect to do ourselves, and to behavior that has clear consequences.
keyPoints: Four related processes: attentional, retention, production, incentive/motivational (Table 13.1).
No modeling without attention; mere exposure is not enough.
Observer must perceive the model accurately enough to imitate.
Celebrities, experts, confident and attractive models draw more attention; TV and YouTube models are powerful.
Attention rises with observer's cognitive skills, knowledge, personal relevance and visible consequences.

sections.heading: Retention Processes
sections.detailed:
To repeat a model's behavior later, we must remember its significant aspects. To retain what we have attended to, we must encode it and represent it symbolically. Bandura described two ways of doing this: an imaginal internal representational system and a verbal representational system.

The imaginal system. While watching the model, we form vivid images that are easy to retrieve. This is the everyday ability that lets you call up a picture of someone you met recently or a place you visited last summer. In observational learning, we form a mental picture of the model's behavior and use it as the basis for imitation at some future time.

The verbal system. This works similarly but involves verbally coding the behavior we observe. During observation we may describe to ourselves what the model is doing. These descriptions or codes can be rehearsed silently, without actually performing the behavior. For example, we might talk ourselves through the steps of a complicated skill, mentally rehearsing the sequence we will carry out later. When we want to perform the action, the verbal code provides hints, reminders and cues.

Together, images and verbal symbols are the means by which we store observed situations and rehearse them for later performance. Table 13.1 describes retention as using cognitive processes to form mental images and verbal descriptions of the model's behavior so we can repeat it later; its example is taking notes on lecture material or on a video of someone driving.

This links back to the age of observers: infants cannot imitate after a delay because these two representational systems have not yet developed.
sections.simple: Retention means remembering what the model did so you can do it later. We store it in two ways: as mental pictures (imaginal system) and as words we say to ourselves (verbal system). We can rehearse these silently, and the words act as cues when we finally perform the behavior.
keyPoints: We must remember significant aspects of the model's behavior to repeat it later.
Observed behavior is encoded and represented symbolically.
Imaginal system: vivid, retrievable mental pictures of the model's behavior.
Verbal system: describing the behavior to ourselves; codes rehearsed silently and used as cues.
Table 13.1 example: taking notes on a driving lecture or video.

sections.heading: Production Processes
sections.detailed:
Production processes translate imaginal and verbal symbolic representations into overt behavior. The chapter describes them more simply as practice. Even after attending to, retaining and rehearsing a model's behavior, we may still be unable to perform it correctly. This is most likely with highly skilled actions that require mastering many component behaviors.

The chapter's example is learning to drive. We pick up the basic motions by watching a model drive, and we may review our symbolic representations many times, but at first our translation of these symbols into real driving is clumsy. We may brake too soon or too late, or overcorrect the steering. Observation alone was not enough for immediate, skilled performance. Practice of the proper physical movements, together with feedback on their accuracy, is needed to produce smooth performance.

Table 13.1 defines production as physically producing the responses and receiving feedback on the accuracy of continued practice; its example is getting into a car with an instructor to practise shifting gears and dodging traffic cones in a school parking lot.

Applying this to a skill such as tennis, as a review question asks: a learner who has watched a coach serve and remembers the sequence still needs to actually hit many serves, receive feedback on grip, toss and swing, and adjust until the observed pattern becomes a smooth, accurate action. The key elements are physical practice and feedback.
sections.simple: Production means turning what you saw and remember into real action, which basically means practice. Watching someone drive doesn't make you a smooth driver; at first you brake too late or oversteer. You need practice plus feedback until the movements become smooth.
keyPoints: Production converts symbolic representations into overt behavior: essentially practice.
Even well-retained behavior may not be performed correctly at first.
Hardest with highly skilled actions made of many component behaviors.
Driving example: early attempts are clumsy (braking, steering).
Physical practice plus feedback on accuracy produces smooth performance.

sections.heading: Incentive and Motivational Processes
sections.detailed:
However well we attend to and retain a behavior, and however capable we are of performing it, we will not perform it without incentive or motivation. When incentives are available, observation is turned into action more quickly. Incentives also affect the earlier processes: without an incentive we may pay less attention, and when we pay less attention there is less to retain.

Anticipation of reinforcement. Our incentive to learn is shaped by what reinforcement or punishment we anticipate. Seeing that a model's behavior earns a reward or avoids a punishment can be a strong incentive to attend to, remember and correctly perform that behavior. The reinforcement is experienced vicariously while we watch the model, and afterwards we expect our own performance to bring the same consequences. Table 13.1 describes this as perceiving that the model's behavior leads to a reward and expecting that our successful performance will bring similar results; its example is expecting to pass the state test and get a driver's license once we master driving.

Reinforcement is not always necessary. Bandura stressed that while reinforcement can make learning easier, it is not always required. Many factors besides reward determine what we attend to, retain and rehearse. Loud sounds, bright lights and exciting videos may capture our interest even though we have never been reinforced for attending to them. His research showed that children watching a model on television or in a video game imitate the model whether or not they have been promised a reward. So reinforcement assists modeling but is not vital to it.

When reinforcement does occur, it can come from three sources: it can be given by another person, experienced vicariously, or administered by oneself. This is Bandura's position on the role of reinforcement in learning, a frequent exam question: reinforcement helps, especially through anticipation of consequences, but learning can occur without it.
sections.simple: Even if you noticed, remembered and can perform a behavior, you won't do it without a reason. Seeing a model get rewarded makes us expect the same, so we're more motivated. But Bandura said reinforcement isn't essential: kids copy TV and video-game models even with no reward promised. Reinforcement can come from others, vicariously, or from yourself.
keyPoints: Without incentive or motivation, learned behavior is not performed.
Incentives speed action and also boost attention and retention.
Anticipated reinforcement, seen vicariously in the model, motivates performance.
Reinforcement helps but is not necessary for learning (loud sounds, bright lights, exciting videos).
Children imitate TV/video-game models with or without promised reward.
Reinforcement can be external, vicarious or self-administered.

sections.heading: Self-Reinforcement and Self-Efficacy: Self-Reinforcement
sections.detailed:
The self in Bandura's theory. Bandura did not see the self as a psychic agent that causes behavior. Instead, the self is a set of cognitive processes and structures concerned with thought and perception. Its two important aspects are self-reinforcement and self-efficacy.

Self-reinforcement. For older children and adults, reinforcement we give ourselves is as important as reinforcement from others. We set personal standards of behavior and achievement, reward ourselves for meeting or exceeding them, and punish ourselves for falling short. Self-administered rewards can be tangible, such as buying yourself new gym shoes or a car, or emotional, such as pride or satisfaction in a job well done. Self-administered punishment shows up as shame, guilt or depression about not behaving as we wished. Self-reinforcement looks conceptually similar to what other theorists call conscience or superego, but Bandura denied that it is the same thing.

How it regulates behavior. A continuing process of self-reinforcement regulates much of our behavior. It requires internal standards of performance, subjective criteria or reference points against which we judge our behavior. Past behavior can become a reference point for judging present behavior and an incentive to do better. When we reach a level of achievement that no longer challenges, motivates or satisfies us, we raise the standard. Failure may lead us to lower the standard to a more realistic level. In this way self-reinforcement changes behavior over time.

Unrealistic performance standards. People who set unrealistic standards, for example because they learned expectations from unusually talented and successful models, may keep trying to meet those excessively high expectations despite repeated failure. They may punish themselves emotionally with feelings of worthlessness and depression, and these feelings can lead to self-destructive behavior such as alcohol and drug abuse or retreat into a fantasy world.

Sources of standards. We learn our initial internal standards, realistic or not, from models, usually parents and teachers. Increasingly we also learn them from online sources such as celebrity blogs and social media. Once we adopt a style of behavior, we begin a lifelong process of comparing our behavior with that of the models. The chapter summary adds that our ultimate goal is to set realistic standards so as to maintain an optimal level of self-efficacy.
sections.simple: For Bandura, the self is just a set of thinking processes, not a hidden agent. We set our own standards, reward ourselves when we meet them and feel guilty or ashamed when we don't. If we copy standards from super-talented models, we may keep failing and spiral into worthlessness, depression or substance abuse.
keyPoints: The self is a set of cognitive processes and structures, not a psychic agent.
Self-reinforcement: rewarding or punishing ourselves against our own standards.
Rewards can be tangible or emotional; punishment appears as shame, guilt, depression.
Similar to conscience/superego, but Bandura said it is not the same.
Standards rise after success and may fall after failure.
Unrealistic standards from very talented models can lead to depression and self-destructive behavior.

sections.heading: Self-Efficacy, or "Believing You Can": Meaning, Low and High Self-Efficacy
sections.detailed:
How well we meet our behavioral standards determines our self-efficacy. In Bandura's system, self-efficacy means feelings of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life. Meeting and maintaining our performance standards raises self-efficacy; failing to meet and maintain them lowers it (Bandura, 2012, 2013).

Bandura also described self-efficacy as our perception of the control we have over our lives. People try to exercise control over events that affect them; by exerting influence where they can, they are better able to bring about the futures they want and prevent the ones they do not. In his view the striving for control runs through almost everything people do. Another psychologist, Maddux (2002), described self-efficacy simply as the power of believing you can, and called this belief one of the most important ingredients in success. Believing that you can succeed is therefore a powerful asset.

Low self-efficacy. People low in self-efficacy feel helpless and unable to control life events, believing any effort is futile. When they hit obstacles, they give up quickly if their first attempt fails. Those extremely low in self-efficacy do not even try, convinced that nothing they do will make a difference. Low self-efficacy can destroy motivation, lower aspirations, interfere with cognitive abilities and harm physical health.

High self-efficacy. People high in self-efficacy believe they can deal effectively with events and situations. Because they expect to overcome obstacles, they persevere and often perform at a high level. They have more confidence in their abilities and little self-doubt. They see difficulties as challenges rather than threats and actively seek new situations. High self-efficacy reduces fear of failure, raises aspirations and improves problem solving and analytical thinking.

This contrast answers the review question on how high and low self-efficacy people differ in coping with life. As an example of using self-efficacy to exert control, a person who believes they can master a difficult subject will keep studying through early setbacks, treat a poor test score as a challenge and seek out new strategies, which in turn makes success more likely.
sections.simple: Self-efficacy is your belief that you can handle life and control what happens to you, the 'power of believing you can'. Low self-efficacy people feel helpless and quit fast or don't try at all. High self-efficacy people keep going, see problems as challenges, fear failure less and think better.
keyPoints: Self-efficacy: feelings of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life.
Meeting standards raises it; failing to meet them lowers it (Bandura, 2012, 2013).
Also described as perceived control over one's life; Maddux (2002): 'power of believing you can'.
Low: helplessness, quick giving up, lower motivation and aspirations, poorer cognition and health.
High: perseverance, high performance, challenges not threats, less fear of failure, better problem solving.

sections.heading: Sources of Information about Self-Efficacy and Ways of Increasing It
sections.detailed:
We judge our self-efficacy from four sources of information: performance attainment, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological and emotional arousal.

Performance attainment. This is the most influential source. Past successes give direct evidence of our mastery and competence, and prior achievements strengthen self-efficacy. Past failures, especially repeated failures in childhood, lower it. Feedback on performance, such as on a work assignment or classroom quiz, is an important indicator. College students solving complicated puzzles who received positive feedback reported higher perceived competence than those given negative feedback (Elliot, Faler, McGregor, Campbell, Sedikides, & Harackiewicz, 2000). Older adults who completed a six-month Tai Chi training program reported significant increases in self-efficacy compared with those who did not (Li, McAuley, Harmer, Duncan, & Chaumeton, 2001). Female college students who completed a 16-hour physical self-defense course showed significantly higher self-efficacy in physical competence, general coping and interpersonal assertiveness, while a control group showed no change (Weitlauf, Cervone, Smith, & Wright, 2001). Put simply, the more we achieve, the more we believe we can achieve.

Vicarious experiences. Seeing others succeed strengthens self-efficacy, especially when they are similar to us in ability; in effect we think that if they can do it, so can we. Seeing others fail can lower it. Effective models are therefore vital, and they also show us useful strategies for difficult situations.

Verbal persuasion. Reminding people that they have the ability to achieve what they want can raise self-efficacy. This may be the most common source, used by parents, teachers, spouses, coaches, friends and therapists. It must be realistic; urging a 5-foot-tall person toward professional basketball is poor advice when another sport such as martial arts would fit better.

Physiological and emotional arousal. How fearful or calm we feel in a stressful situation is used to judge our ability to cope. We are more confident of mastering a problem when we are not agitated, tense or troubled by headaches. The calmer we feel, the higher our self-efficacy; the higher our arousal, fear, anxiety or tension, the lower it is.

Ways of increasing self-efficacy. Bandura concluded that self-efficacy can be raised by: (1) arranging reachable goals so people have success experiences, increasing performance attainment; (2) exposing people to appropriate successful models, enhancing vicarious success; (3) providing verbal persuasion so people believe they can succeed; and (4) strengthening physiological arousal through proper diet, stress reduction and exercise, increasing strength, stamina and coping ability. He used these conditions to help people learn musical instruments, relate better to the opposite sex, master computer skills, quit smoking, and conquer phobias and physical pain.
sections.simple: We judge our self-efficacy from four things: our own past successes (the strongest), seeing similar people succeed, being told 'you can do it' (realistically), and how calm or anxious our body feels. To boost it, set reachable goals, show good models, give encouragement, and improve physical condition through diet, stress reduction and exercise.
keyPoints: Four sources: performance attainment, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, physiological/emotional arousal.
Performance attainment is the most influential (feedback, Tai Chi and self-defense studies).
Vicarious experience works best with models similar in ability.
Verbal persuasion is probably the most common source but must be realistic.
Calm states raise self-efficacy; high arousal lowers it.
Increase it via reachable goals, successful models, persuasion, and diet, stress reduction, exercise.

sections.heading: Developmental Stages of Self-Efficacy: Childhood
sections.detailed:
Self-efficacy develops gradually. Infants begin to build it as they try to exert more influence over their physical and social environments. They learn about the consequences of their own abilities, such as physical prowess, social skills and language competence. These abilities are used almost constantly to act on the environment, mainly through their effects on parents. Ideally, parents respond to the child's activities and attempts to communicate and provide stimulating surroundings that give the child freedom to grow and explore.

Parents and gender. Early efficacy-building experiences centre on the parents, and the parental behaviors that lead to high self-efficacy differ for boys and girls. High self-efficacy men tended to have had warm relationships with their fathers as children, while their mothers were more demanding than their fathers, expecting higher performance and achievement. High self-efficacy women, by contrast, experienced pressure from their fathers for high achievement during childhood (Schneewind, 1995).

Reduction of parental influence. Parental influence shrinks as the child's world widens to include siblings, peers and other adults. Like Adler, Bandura considered birth order important: first-born and only children have different bases for judging their abilities than later-born children. Siblings of the same sex tend to be more competitive than opposite-sex siblings, which also affects self-efficacy. Among playmates, the most experienced and successful children serve as high-efficacy models, and peers provide comparison points for judging one's own achievement.

Teachers. Teachers influence self-efficacy through their effect on the development of cognitive abilities and problem-solving skills, which are vital for adult functioning. Children often rate their own competence according to their teachers' evaluations. Bandura argued that schools using ability groupings undermine the self-efficacy and self-confidence of students placed in the lower groups, and that competitive practices such as grading on a curve condemn poor achievers to average or low grades.
sections.simple: Babies start building self-efficacy by seeing that their actions affect the world, especially their parents. Responsive parents help. Later, siblings, birth order, peers and teachers matter more. Bandura thought ability grouping and grading on a curve hurt the self-efficacy of weaker students.
keyPoints: Infants build self-efficacy by influencing their environment, mainly parents.
Responsive parents and stimulating surroundings help.
High self-efficacy men: warm fathers, more demanding mothers; women: fathers pushing achievement (Schneewind, 1995).
Parental influence declines as siblings, peers and other adults enter; birth order matters (as for Adler).
Same-sex siblings compete more; successful playmates act as high-efficacy models.
Teachers shape self-efficacy; ability grouping and grading on a curve undermine low achievers.

sections.heading: Developmental Stages of Self-Efficacy: Adolescence, Adulthood and Old Age
sections.detailed:
Adolescence. The transitional experiences of adolescence involve new demands and pressures, from a growing awareness of sex to choosing a college and career. Adolescents must develop new competencies and new appraisals of their abilities. Bandura noted that success at this stage typically depends on the level of self-efficacy built up during childhood.

Adulthood. Bandura divided adulthood into young adulthood and the middle years. Young adulthood brings new adjustments such as marriage, parenthood and establishing a career. High self-efficacy is needed for these to go well; people low in self-efficacy will not cope adequately and are likely to fail to adjust.

Women who feel highly efficacious about their parenting skills are likely to promote self-efficacy in their children. Women who believe they are good parents are less prone to despondency and emotional strain in the parenting role than women low in self-efficacy (Olioff & Aboud, 1991; Teti & Gelfand, 1991). High self-efficacy mothers working outside the home experienced significantly less physical and emotional strain from work-family conflicts than low self-efficacy mothers (Bandura, 1995).

The middle years are also stressful, as people reevaluate their careers and their family and social lives. As we face our limitations and redefine our goals, we must reassess our skills and find new opportunities for enhancing self-efficacy.

Old age. Self-efficacy reassessment in old age is difficult. Declining mental and physical abilities, retirement and withdrawal from social life may force a new round of self-appraisal. Lower self-efficacy can further impair physical and mental functioning in a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy; for example, reduced confidence about sexual performance can lead to less sexual activity. Lower physical efficacy can bring fatigue and a cutting back of physical activities. If we no longer believe we can do something we used to enjoy and do well, we may stop trying.

Bandura's conclusion is that self-efficacy is the single most important factor in determining success or failure across the entire life span.
sections.simple: Teens face new pressures like sex and career choice, and cope better if they built strong self-efficacy as kids. Young adults need it for marriage, parenting and careers; middle-aged adults must reassess goals. In old age, declining abilities can lower self-efficacy, which then makes people do even less, like a self-fulfilling prophecy.
keyPoints: Adolescence: new demands (sex, college, career); success depends on childhood self-efficacy.
Young adulthood: marriage, parenthood, career require high self-efficacy.
High self-efficacy mothers promote it in children and suffer less strain (Olioff & Aboud; Teti & Gelfand; Bandura, 1995).
Middle years: reevaluation of career, family and social life.
Old age: decline and retirement force reappraisal; low efficacy acts as a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Self-efficacy is the single most important factor in success or failure across the life span.

sections.heading: Behavior Modification: Fears and Phobias
sections.detailed:
Bandura's aim in developing his social-cognitive theory was to modify learned behaviors that society considers undesirable or abnormal. Like Skinner, he focused on external aspects, the inappropriate or destructive behaviors themselves, believing that they are learned just as all behaviors are. He did not try to deal with supposed underlying unconscious conflicts. The target of the social-learning approach is the behavior or symptom, not any presumed internal neurosis. This also answers how Bandura deals with the unconscious: he does not use it.

Bandura developed three forms of behavior therapy: modeling, guided participation and covert modeling, applied to fears, phobias and anxieties.

Modeling. If modeling is how we learn behaviors in the first place, it should also be an effective way to relearn them. In an early study (Bandura, Grusec, & Menlove, 1967), children afraid of dogs watched a same-age child play with a dog. From a safe distance, they saw the model make progressively bolder moves: petting the dog through the bars of a playpen, then going inside and playing with it. The observers' fear of dogs was considerably reduced.

In a classic study of snake phobia (Bandura, Blanchard, & Ritter, 1969), adults with intense fear of snakes watched a film in which children, adolescents and adults made progressively closer contact with a snake: first handling plastic snakes, then touching live ones, and finally letting a large snake crawl over their bodies. Participants could stop the film whenever it became too threatening. Gradually, their fear was overcome. This is a typical example of an experiment using modeling to change behavior.

Guided participation. Here the person watches a live model and then participates with the model. For snake phobia, participants watch through an observation window as a live model handles a snake, then enter the room and watch at close range. Wearing gloves, they are coaxed into touching the middle of the snake while the model holds its head and tail, and eventually they touch the snake without gloves.

Covert modeling. Modeling works even without an observable model. In covert modeling, people are told to imagine a model coping with the feared or threatening situation; they never actually see one. It has been used successfully for snake phobias and social inhibitions.

Why it matters. Overcoming a fear of snakes has changed many people's lives, even those who rarely meet snakes. Besides boosting self-esteem and self-efficacy, it can alter personal and work habits. One woman could wear a necklace for the first time, having avoided necklaces because they reminded her of snakes. A realtor increased his income because he no longer feared visiting rural properties. Many others were freed from snake nightmares. Phobias restrict daily life; many people who fear spiders react with rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath and vomiting just from a picture. Phobics doubt their self-efficacy in these situations, so relieving their fears expands their environment and increases self-efficacy.
sections.simple: Bandura used modeling to fix unwanted learned behavior, targeting the behavior itself, not hidden unconscious conflicts. Kids scared of dogs and adults scared of snakes lost their fear after watching models get gradually closer. In guided participation you watch a live model and then join in; in covert modeling you just imagine a model coping.
keyPoints: Goal: modify learned behaviors society sees as undesirable; target is the symptom, not unconscious conflict.
Three therapies: modeling, guided participation, covert modeling.
Bandura, Grusec & Menlove (1967): fear of dogs reduced by watching a peer model.
Bandura, Blanchard & Ritter (1969): filmed graduated snake contact cured snake phobia.
Guided participation: watch a live model, then handle the snake with the model (gloves, then none).
Covert modeling: imagine a model coping; used for snake phobias and social inhibitions.

sections.heading: Advantages of Modeling Therapy
sections.detailed:
Modeling therapy, especially when it uses online video techniques, has several practical advantages. Complex behaviors can be seen as a whole. Extraneous behaviors can be edited out, so the client's time is spent viewing only relevant behavior. The same videos can be shown to many patients and used by several therapists at the same time. Modeling techniques can also be used with groups, saving time and money when treating people with the same problem.

Effectiveness. The approach has been effective with phobias, obsessive-compulsive disorders and sexual dysfunction, and the positive effects have been reported to last for years.

Self-efficacy in therapy. A great deal of research has examined self-efficacy during and after behavior-modification therapy. The results show that as clients' self-efficacy improved during treatment, they became increasingly able to deal with the source of their fear. It was the therapeutic procedure itself that raised self-efficacy. This links Bandura's therapy directly to his central cognitive concept: modeling therapy works partly because it builds belief in one's ability to cope.

In short, modeling therapy is efficient (whole behaviors, edited content), economical (repeatable videos, many therapists, groups), effective across several disorders, durable, and self-efficacy enhancing.
sections.simple: Modeling therapy, especially with videos, is practical: you see the whole behavior, irrelevant parts are cut, the same video can be reused with many people, and groups can be treated together. It works for phobias, OCD and sexual dysfunction, the effects last for years, and the therapy itself boosts self-efficacy.
keyPoints: Video modeling shows complex behavior as a whole and edits out irrelevant parts.
Same videos reusable with many patients and therapists; group use saves time and money.
Effective for phobias, obsessive-compulsive disorders, sexual dysfunction.
Positive effects reported to last for years.
As self-efficacy rose during treatment, clients coped better; the procedure itself raised self-efficacy.

sections.heading: Anxiety: Fear of Medical Treatment and Test Anxiety
sections.detailed:
Many behaviors can be modified through modeling. The chapter gives two instances involving anxiety: fear of medical treatment and test anxiety.

Fear of medical treatment. Some people fear medical situations so intensely that they avoid treatment. In an early study (Melamed & Siegel, 1975), children scheduled for surgery who had never been in hospital were divided into two groups. The experimental group watched a film about a boy's hospital experience; the control group watched a film about a boy taking a trip. The boy in the hospital film was an exemplary model: despite some initial anxiety, he coped well with the doctors and procedures. The modeling film reduced anxiety, and children who saw it also had fewer behavior problems after hospitalization than the controls.

Similar procedures have reduced fear of hospitalization in adults and fear of dental treatment. One study involved a medical procedure so stressful that more than 80 percent of patients initially refused it or quit early (Allen, Danforth, & Drabman, 1989). Patients who watched a video of a model undergoing the procedure and describing how he coped with his distress were more likely to complete it, with less anxiety and a shorter hospital stay.

Test anxiety. For some college students, test anxiety is so severe that exam scores do not reflect what they know. In a classic study (Sarason, 1975), students were divided by personality test scores into high and low test-anxiety groups. Some saw a filmed model talk about her test anxiety and how she dealt with it; others saw the same model talk about test anxiety without mentioning coping; a third group saw her talk about other college activities. All then memorised nonsense syllables and were tested on recall. High-anxiety students were most strongly affected by the model who described coping mechanisms and performed significantly better than high-anxiety students in the other two conditions.

These studies give ready examples for the review question on how modeling can reduce anxiety: a model who first shows some anxiety and then copes successfully is especially effective.
sections.simple: Modeling also reduces anxiety. Kids who watched a film of a boy coping well in hospital were less anxious before surgery and had fewer problems afterwards. Adults facing a scary procedure did better after watching a coping model. Highly test-anxious students recalled more after seeing a model explain how she handled test anxiety.
keyPoints: Melamed & Siegel (1975): hospital-coping film reduced children's pre-surgery anxiety and later behavior problems.
Similar methods reduce adults' fear of hospitals and dental treatment.
Allen, Danforth & Drabman (1989): coping-model video led to completion, less anxiety, shorter stay.
Sarason (1975): high test-anxiety students did best after a model described coping mechanisms.
Coping models (anxious at first, then coping) are particularly effective.

sections.heading: Ethical Issues in Behavior Modification
sections.detailed:
Despite its impressive results, behavior modification has been criticised by some educators, politicians and psychologists. Their charge is that it exploits people, manipulating and controlling them against their will. Bandura argued that these charges are misleading and answered them on several grounds.

Awareness. Behavior modification does not happen without the client's awareness. Self-awareness and self-regulation are essential for any program to change or relearn behavior to work. Techniques will not succeed unless the person understands which behaviors are being reinforced. So clients are not treated against their will.

Client choice. Clients themselves decide what they want to change; nobody else controls them. People come to a therapist to get rid of specific fears and anxieties that limit their ability to function or cope with daily life. Bandura described the client-therapist relationship as a contract between two consenting individuals, not a relationship between a sinister master-controller and a spineless puppet.

Increased freedom. Far from manipulating or enslaving people, modeling techniques actually increase personal freedom. People who are afraid to leave the house, or who feel compelled to wash their hands continually, are not truly free; they live within the constraints of their phobic or compulsive behavior, which leave them little choice. Removing those constraints through behavior modification increases feelings of freedom and the opportunity for personal growth.

Many techniques derived from Bandura's work have become popular alternatives to psychoanalysis and other therapies. The chapter summary repeats the key defence: with self-awareness and self-regulation, people in behavior modification understand what is being reinforced.
sections.simple: Critics said behavior modification manipulates people against their will. Bandura disagreed: it only works if clients understand what's being reinforced, clients choose what to change, and the therapy is a contract between consenting people. It actually increases freedom by removing the limits that phobias and compulsions impose.
keyPoints: Critics: behavior modification exploits, manipulates and controls people against their will.
Bandura: it requires client awareness, self-awareness and self-regulation.
Clients decide what to change; therapy is a contract between consenting individuals.
Not 'master-controller and puppet'.
Removing phobic/compulsive constraints increases freedom and growth.
Bandura's techniques became popular alternatives to psychoanalysis.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Free will versus determinism. Bandura's position is clear. Behavior is controlled both by the person, through cognitive processes, and by the environment, through external social situations. He called this view reciprocal determinism, defined in the glossary as the idea that behavior is controlled or determined by the individual through cognitive processes and by the environment through external social stimulus events. Bandura noted that people are neither powerless objects controlled by environmental forces nor free agents who can become whatever they choose; people and their environments are reciprocal determinants of each other (1977). So he takes a middle position: neither strict determinism nor unlimited free will.

Nature versus nurture. The chapter summary states Bandura's view that most behavior is learned and that genetic factors play only a minor role. Environment (learning, especially from models) therefore outweighs heredity.

Past versus present. Learning in childhood may be more influential than learning in adulthood, but adults are not victims of their childhood experiences; they can continue to learn and change, as his therapy shows.

Ultimate goal. According to the summary, our ultimate goal is to set realistic performance standards so as to maintain an optimal level of self-efficacy.

Other implications follow from the chapter as a whole. Because cognition mediates behavior and people can regulate themselves through self-reinforcement and self-efficacy, Bandura's image of human nature is more active and hopeful than Skinner's. Behavior can be changed throughout life, including through modeling, guided participation and covert modeling, and the striving for control over life circumstances runs through almost everything people do.
sections.simple: Bandura took a middle path called reciprocal determinism: our thoughts and our environment control each other and our behavior, so we're neither puppets nor totally free. Most behavior is learned and genes play only a small role. Childhood learning matters, but adults aren't stuck with it, and our aim should be realistic standards that keep self-efficacy high.
keyPoints: Reciprocal determinism: behavior controlled by the person (cognition) and the environment (social events).
People are neither powerless objects nor totally free agents (Bandura, 1977).
Most behavior is learned; heredity plays a minor role.
Childhood learning may matter more, but adults are not victims of childhood.
Ultimate goal: realistic standards to maintain optimal self-efficacy.

sections.heading: Assessment in Bandura's Theory
sections.detailed:
Like Skinner, Bandura focused on overt behavior rather than internal motivating variables. He did not use assessment methods such as free association, dream analysis or projective techniques, which are associated with psychoanalytic and related approaches. Unlike Skinner, however, Bandura accepted the operation of cognitive variables, and both these cognitive variables and behavior can be assessed.

The chapter illustrates with studies already described. In the modeling study with children about to undergo surgery, assessment included direct observation of behavior, self-report inventories and physiological measurements. In self-efficacy studies, behavioral and cognitive variables were measured quantitatively. Self-efficacy regarding phobias was assessed through participants' self-ratings of how many tasks on a behavioral-avoidance test they expected to complete. College students' test anxiety was measured with personality inventories.

The conclusion is that assessment of both behavioral and cognitive variables is important in the social-learning approach. The chapter summary lists Bandura's three main methods as direct observation, self-report inventories and physiological measures.

For comparison: Freud relied on free association and dreams, Skinner on behavioral observation of overt responses, and Bandura combined behavioral observation with quantitative measurement of cognitions such as self-efficacy expectations.
sections.simple: Bandura, like Skinner, studied visible behavior and avoided free association, dream analysis and projective tests. Unlike Skinner, he also measured thoughts such as self-efficacy. He used direct observation, self-report inventories and physiological measures, and rated self-efficacy by asking people how many feared tasks they expected to complete.
keyPoints: Focus on overt behavior; no free association, dream analysis or projective techniques.
Unlike Skinner, also assesses cognitive variables.
Methods: direct observation, self-report inventories, physiological measurements.
Phobia self-efficacy: self-rated number of behavioral-avoidance test tasks expected to be completed.
Test anxiety measured by personality inventories.

sections.heading: Research on Bandura's Theory: Self-Efficacy, Age, Gender and Parental Self-Efficacy
sections.detailed:
Research style. Bandura favored well-controlled laboratory investigations in the rigorous tradition of experimental psychology. He used experimental and control groups, measured independent and dependent variables precisely, studied large groups of participants and compared their average performance using statistical analysis. The chapter illustrates the research his theory generated with studies on self-efficacy, collective efficacy and the effects of televised models on aggression.

Age and gender differences. Self-efficacy varies with gender and age. On average, men score higher than women, and this gender difference peaks in the 20s and declines later. For both sexes, self-efficacy rises through childhood and early adulthood, peaks in middle age and declines after 60 (Gecas, 1989; Lachman, 1985).

Individual differences remain large, however. In a study of Dutch adults averaging 66 years, those who believed their memory was getting worse performed significantly worse on memory tests six years later than those with high memory self-efficacy (Valentijn et al., 2006). An analysis of more than 100 studies confirmed that low memory self-efficacy, our belief about how good our memory is, can affect memory test performance (Beaudoin & Desrichard, 2011). Belief in our abilities may actually affect those abilities.

Parental self-efficacy. In Italy, adolescents whose parents believed they were effective parents had higher self-efficacy themselves, fewer behavior problems, less anxiety, better school performance and more open, honest communication with their parents (Steca, Bassi, Caprara, & Fave, 2011). Among African-American teenage boys in a public housing project, higher parental support, control and self-efficacy went with higher self-efficacy in the boys; lack of parental support and guidance and low parental self-efficacy led to more substance abuse and delinquency (Nebbitt, 2009). Among Chicago teenagers, the more supportive the parents, the higher the children's self-efficacy (McCoy & Bowen, 2014). In Mexican-American families, high parental self-efficacy was linked to higher self-efficacy and fewer behavior problems in both male and female adolescents (Dumka, Gonzales, Wheeler, & Millsap, 2010). American young adults whose parents had exercised tight control showed lower self-efficacy than those with less controlling parents (Givertz & Segrin, 2014). In Malaysia, fathers' involvement was as important as mothers' for teenagers' self-efficacy and happiness (Yap & Baharudin, 2015).
sections.simple: Bandura used tightly controlled lab experiments with large groups and statistics. Men score higher in self-efficacy than women, especially in their 20s, and self-efficacy rises until middle age then drops after 60. Believing your memory is good actually helps it. Kids of confident, supportive (but not over-controlling) parents have higher self-efficacy, and dads matter as much as moms.
keyPoints: Research style: controlled lab experiments, experimental/control groups, large samples, statistics.
Men score higher than women; gap peaks in the 20s (Gecas, 1989; Lachman, 1985).
Self-efficacy rises to a peak in middle age and declines after 60.
Memory self-efficacy predicts later memory performance (Valentijn et al., 2006; Beaudoin & Desrichard, 2011).
High parental self-efficacy and support raise teens' self-efficacy across Italy, US, Mexican-American families.
Tight parental control lowers self-efficacy (Givertz & Segrin, 2014); fathers matter as much as mothers (Yap & Baharudin, 2015).

sections.heading: Research on Self-Efficacy: Physical Appearance, Academic Performance and Culture
sections.detailed:
Physical appearance. Appearance can affect the reinforcers people get from others and so how they feel about themselves. In adults aged 25 to 76, physical appearance had a greater effect on feelings of being in control of their lives than either self-esteem or health (Andreoletti, Zebrowitz, & Lachman, 2001). Baby-faceness, a round face, large eyes, small nose bridge and small chin, was strongly related to low control beliefs in young and middle adulthood. Older baby-faced adults, however, reported stronger feelings of control, perhaps because they looked younger than thin-faced people their age and were treated differently; the findings were stronger for women, and a youthful appearance later in life had social and workplace advantages. People rated less attractive reported lower feelings of control at work and socially, and shorter people reported lower feelings of control in young adulthood than taller or average-height people.

Academic performance. Self-efficacy and academic performance are significantly and positively related. Teachers high in self-efficacy create more opportunities for students to achieve. Students' self-efficacy is positively related to motivation, effort, aspiration and persistence in class (Bassi, Steca, Fave, & Caprara, 2007; Gibson & Dembo, 1984; Multon, Brown, & Lent, 1991; Zimmerman, 1995). German teachers high in self-efficacy were rated by students as more effective, and teachers rated highly by students then developed even higher self-efficacy, since the positive feedback reinforced their confidence (Holzberger, Philipp, & Kunter, 2013).

Bandura (1997) also found that schools differ in how they build self-efficacy. In high-achieving schools, principals cared more about education than about enforcing policies and rules, and teachers set high expectations and standards. In low-achieving schools, principals acted more as administrators and disciplinarians than educators, and teachers expected little academically.

Cultural differences. Before German reunification in 1990, elementary students in grades two to six in communist-collectivist East Germany scored lower in self-efficacy than those in capitalist-individualist West Germany, with less confidence in their school ability and lower ratings of their own intelligence (Oettingen & Maier, 1999). In Iran, high school students with a stronger sense of ethnic identity had higher self-efficacy than those with a weak ethnic identity (Hejazi & Hasany, 2014).
sections.simple: Looks affect how in control people feel: baby-faced, less attractive and shorter young adults feel less control, though baby-faced older adults feel more. Confident teachers and students do better, and good schools have education-focused principals with high expectations. Kids in individualist West Germany had higher self-efficacy than those in collectivist East Germany.
keyPoints: Appearance affected control beliefs more than self-esteem or health (Andreoletti et al., 2001).
Baby-faceness linked to low control when young but higher control when older; stronger for women.
Less attractive and shorter people reported lower control.
Self-efficacy positively related to academic performance, motivation, effort, persistence.
High-efficacy German teachers rated more effective, and good ratings raised their efficacy (Holzberger et al., 2013).
Culture: East German children lower than West (Oettingen & Maier, 1999); ethnic identity raises it in Iran (Hejazi & Hasany, 2014).

sections.heading: Research on Self-Efficacy: Career Choice and Job Performance
sections.detailed:
Gender and career choice. Gender differences in self-efficacy can shape career choice. Men see themselves as high in self-efficacy for both traditionally male and traditionally female occupations. Women see themselves as high in self-efficacy for traditionally female occupations but low for traditionally male ones. Yet the men and women in this research performed at comparable levels on standardized tests of verbal and quantitative skills. They had similar measurable abilities but perceived them differently, so their feelings of competence for careers differed by gender (Hackett, 1995).

Job hunting and goals. Self-efficacy affects the time spent job hunting and later job success. Employees high in self-efficacy set higher personal goals and are more committed to them. They focus on analysing and solving problems at work, while low self-efficacy employees focus on personal deficiencies and fear of failure, which can undermine productivity (Locke & Latham, 1990). Failure at a computer-based task was shown to reduce self-efficacy (Hardy, 2014).

Job performance. A meta-analysis of 114 studies with more than 21,600 participants supported a significant positive relationship: the higher the self-efficacy, the better the job performance (Stajkovic & Luthans, 1998). An update found self-efficacy predicted performance better for low-complexity jobs than for medium- or high-complexity jobs (Judge, Jackson, Shaw, Scott, & Rich, 2007). High self-efficacy people are also more fully engaged in their work and experience less burnout (Ventura, Salanova, & Llorens, 2015).

Feedback. High self-efficacy people perform better when they receive more feedback about their performance and often do poorly when there is little or none; not knowing how they are doing can be a negative factor for them (Schmidt & DeShon, 2010). People high in self-efficacy are also more successful in job training programs and report higher job satisfaction, organizational commitment and job performance (Gupta, Ganster, & Kepes, 2013; Salas & Cannon-Bowers, 2001).
