sections.simple: Men feel capable of both 'male' and 'female' jobs, but women feel capable mainly of 'female' jobs, even though their tested abilities are the same. High self-efficacy workers set higher goals, solve problems, perform better (especially in simpler jobs), burn out less and like their jobs more, but they need feedback to do their best.
keyPoints: Women feel low efficacy for traditionally male jobs despite equal tested abilities (Hackett, 1995).
High self-efficacy employees set higher goals and focus on problem solving (Locke & Latham, 1990).
Failing a computer task lowers self-efficacy (Hardy, 2014).
Meta-analysis of 114 studies: higher self-efficacy, better job performance (Stajkovic & Luthans, 1998).
Stronger predictor for low-complexity jobs (Judge et al., 2007); less burnout (Ventura et al., 2015).
High self-efficacy people need feedback (Schmidt & DeShon, 2010); do better in training, more satisfied.

sections.heading: Research on Self-Efficacy: Physical Health
sections.detailed:
Self-efficacy affects physical well-being, including pain tolerance, a healthy lifestyle and recovery from illness.

Pain tolerance. Pregnant women taught relaxation and breathing exercises believed they had more control over childbirth pain than women not taught these techniques. The higher their self-efficacy and sense of control, the longer they tolerated discomfort before asking for medication, and the less medication they needed (Manning & Wright, 1983). In a study of more than 15,000 patients in China, those higher in self-efficacy had less impairment, emotional distress and pain severity (Jackson, Wang, Wang, & Fan, 2014). Coping techniques that improve self-efficacy substantially increase endorphins, the body's natural painkillers. Patients with low back pain in a three-week rehabilitation program were given pain and self-efficacy rating scales; six months later, those higher in self-efficacy reported better physical functioning and less pain (Altmaier, Russell, Kao, Lehmann, & Weinstein, 1993).

Maintaining a healthy lifestyle. Bandura wrote that lifestyle habits can enhance or impair health and that efficacy beliefs affect every phase of personal change: whether people consider changing health habits, whether they find the motivation and perseverance to succeed, and how well they maintain the change (Bandura, 1995). Techniques for enhancing self-efficacy in adults aged 60 and older increased their physical activity, while those whose self-efficacy stayed low led more sedentary, unhealthy lives (French, Olander, Chrisholm, & McSharry, 2014). Among Native American and native Alaskan adults, the lower the self-efficacy, the greater the alcohol consumption (Taylor, 2000). Adolescents higher in self-efficacy were more resistant to peer pressure to start smoking (Schwarzer & Fuchs, 1995; Stacy, Sussman, Dent, Burton, & Floy, 1992).

Recovering from illness. People high in self-efficacy responded better to cognitive and behavioral treatment for pulmonary disease. Men who had heart attacks returned to normal activities more often, with less fear and depression, when both they and their spouses believed in their cardiac fitness. The higher the patients' self-efficacy, the more they followed prescribed exercise programs and the more they improved (Kaplan, Atkins, & Reinsch, 1984; McLeod, 1986). A large study of heart patients in Italy confirmed that higher self-efficacy eased the impact of illness and raised health satisfaction (Greco, Steca, Monzani, Malfatto, & Parati, 2015). In Israel, diabetes patients high in self-efficacy were far more likely to persist with self-care (Mishali, Omer, & Heymann, 2011). Orthopedic surgery patients (hip or knee replacement) high in self-efficacy did significantly better in rehabilitation (Waldrop, Lightsey, Ethington, Woemmel, & Coke, 2001). Breast cancer patients who more strongly expected to remain cancer-free showed better emotional adjustment (Carver et al., 2000).
sections.simple: High self-efficacy helps the body: people tolerate pain better and need less medication, stick to healthy habits, drink and smoke less, and recover better from heart attacks, lung disease, diabetes, surgery and cancer. Self-efficacy even boosts endorphins, the body's natural painkillers.
keyPoints: Childbirth: higher self-efficacy, longer tolerance and less medication (Manning & Wright, 1983).
Chinese patients and back-pain patients: higher self-efficacy, less pain (Jackson et al., 2014; Altmaier et al., 1993).
Self-efficacy-boosting coping raises endorphins.
Efficacy beliefs affect every phase of health-habit change (Bandura, 1995); more activity in over-60s (French et al., 2014).
Lower self-efficacy, more alcohol (Taylor, 2000); higher self-efficacy resists smoking (Schwarzer & Fuchs; Stacy et al.).
Better recovery: heart, pulmonary, diabetes, orthopedic surgery, breast cancer adjustment.

sections.heading: Research on Self-Efficacy: Mental Health and Coping with Stress
sections.detailed:
Depression and anxiety. In Italy, children averaging 11.5 years who rated themselves low in social and academic efficacy were significantly more likely to be depressed than high-efficacy children; low social efficacy was also significantly related to depression among US adolescents (Bandura, Pastorelli, Barbarelli, & Caprara, 1999). In the Netherlands, low social efficacy in adolescents was related to high anxiety, neuroticism and depressive symptoms (Muris, 2002). Studies in China and Nigeria found that high self-efficacy people experienced less on-the-job stress and less test anxiety (Li, 2010; Onyeizugbo, 2010). Among adults, low social efficacy contributed to depression partly because a lack of coping skills hindered the development of a social support network (Holahan & Holahan, 1987). The relationship may be circular rather than simple cause and effect: low self-efficacy can lead to depression, and depression further reduces self-efficacy. Depressed people believe they are far less capable than others and have little control over their situations (Bandura, 1997).

Social interest and self-esteem. American college students high in self-efficacy also scored higher on several characteristics of mental health proposed by Adler: social interest, the desire to strive for perfection, and a sense of belonging (Dinter, 2000). In Canada, Iran and the United States, high school students and adults high in self-efficacy also tended to score high in self-esteem and were less likely to procrastinate or give up when facing obstacles (Hoseinzadah, Azizi, & Tavakoli, 2014; Lightsey, Burke, Ervin, Henderson, & Yee, 2006; Steel, 2007).

Coping with stress. Enhanced self-efficacy and a sense of control are positively related to coping with stress and minimising its harmful biological effects. Bandura (2001) wrote that strong coping efficacy reduces vulnerability to stress and depression and strengthens resilience. High self-efficacy has been associated with a stronger immune system, lower release of stress-related hormones and reduced susceptibility to respiratory infections.

Women higher in self-efficacy coped better with the stress of abortion, with significantly less depression and better mood (Cozzarelli, 1993), and coped better with the demands following the birth of a first child (Ozer, 1995). Refugees migrating from East to West Germany after the Berlin Wall fell in 1990 adapted significantly better to the shift from a disadvantaged communist lifestyle to an affluent capitalist one when they were high in self-efficacy; they saw the demands as challenges rather than threats and had lower anxiety, better health and fewer health complaints (Jerusalem & Mittag, 1995). Among Dutch adults facially disfigured by treatment for head or neck cancer, those lower in self-efficacy experienced more stress in response to unpleasant or rejecting behavior from others, while those higher in self-efficacy felt they could exercise some control over how others reacted (Hagedoorn & Molleman, 2006).
sections.simple: Low self-efficacy goes with depression, anxiety and neuroticism, and depression lowers self-efficacy further, a vicious circle. High self-efficacy goes with Adler-style social interest, higher self-esteem and less procrastination. It also helps people handle stress, from abortion and new motherhood to migration and disfigurement, and even strengthens the immune system.
keyPoints: Low social/academic efficacy linked to depression in children and teens (Bandura et al., 1999; Muris, 2002).
High self-efficacy: less job stress and test anxiety in China and Nigeria (Li, 2010; Onyeizugbo, 2010).
Self-efficacy and depression may be circular (Holahan & Holahan, 1987; Bandura, 1997).
High self-efficacy linked to Adler's social interest and belonging (Dinter, 2000) and higher self-esteem, less procrastination.
Stress: stronger immunity, fewer stress hormones, fewer respiratory infections.
Better coping with abortion, first childbirth, migration and facial disfigurement.

sections.heading: Collective Efficacy
sections.detailed:
Just as an individual develops self-efficacy, a group working together toward specific goals can develop collective efficacy (Dithurbide & Feltz, 2012): the shared feeling that the group can overcome obstacles and reach its goals. Examples include a sports team, a department in a large organization, a military combat unit, or neighbors uniting to fight drug dealers.

Sports. In college basketball, high collective efficacy arose in teams that had highly competent leaders early in the season and had won most of their games the previous season. Teams highest in collective efficacy at the start of the new season finished better in end-of-season standings than teams low in collective efficacy (Watson, Chemers, & Preiser, 2001).

Family and schools. High collective efficacy in families leads to more open family communication, more truthful disclosure by teenagers to parents and greater satisfaction with family life for parents and children (Bandura, Caprara, Barbaranelli, Regalia, & Scabini, 2011). High collective efficacy among teachers in the Netherlands led to higher student achievement and better grades (Moolenaar, Sleegers, & Daly, 2012). Higher collective efficacy among 5th-, 8th- and 11th-grade US students reduced bullying (Williams & Guerra, 2011). In Greece, 11- to 14-year-olds in classes high in collective efficacy showed and received far less bullying than those in low collective efficacy classes (Sapouna, 2010).

Neighborhoods and organizations. High collective efficacy in a neighborhood, even a tough inner-city one, has been related to decreases in alcoholism, drug use, violence and criminal behavior including murder (Ahern et al., 2013; Fagan, Wright, & Pinchevsky, 2014; Maxwell, Garner, & Skogan, 2011). In employing organizations, collective efficacy increases on-the-job performance and helping behavior and reduces workplace stress, in Western cultures and in China (Du, Shin, & Choi, 2015; Esnard & Roques, 2014). In Italy, air force personnel in units with higher collective efficacy showed greater organizational commitment and job satisfaction (Borgogni, Petitta, & Mastrorilla, 2010).

In summary, groups high in collective efficacy win more games, get better grades, show more commitment, job satisfaction and performance, bully less and have more open, satisfying family relationships.
sections.simple: Collective efficacy is a group's shared belief that together it can succeed. Basketball teams high in it finished better; families high in it talk more openly; classes high in it bully less; neighborhoods high in it have less crime and drug use; and workplaces high in it perform better with less stress.
keyPoints: Collective efficacy: a group's shared sense that it can overcome obstacles and reach goals (Dithurbide & Feltz, 2012).
Basketball teams with competent leaders and past wins had high collective efficacy and finished better (Watson et al., 2001).
Families: more open communication and satisfaction (Bandura et al., 2011).
Schools: higher grades (teachers) and less bullying (Williams & Guerra; Sapouna).
Neighborhoods: less alcoholism, drugs, violence and crime.
Organizations: better performance, helping, less stress; Italian air force more committed and satisfied.

sections.heading: Self-Efficacy and the Internet
sections.detailed:
Internet self-efficacy is our confidence in our ability to use the Internet effectively. The chapter summary adds that computer self-efficacy strongly influences our online behavior.

Gender. Among 8th-grade students in Taiwan, there were no overall gender differences in Internet self-efficacy, but girls were more confident than boys in communicating online, while boys were more confident in exploring online (Tsai & Tsai, 2010). (The chapter's highlights box summarises this as Taiwanese 8th-grade girls scoring higher than boys.) Among American college students, men ranked higher in computer self-efficacy than women (Buse, 2010).

Social self-efficacy and Internet addiction. College students in Turkey high in social self-efficacy, confidence in initiating social contact and making friends easily, had greater self-esteem and emotional well-being but were far more likely to become addicted to Internet use than those low in social self-efficacy (Iskender & Akin, 2010).

Self-presentation online. German adults high in self-efficacy about making a favorable impression on others posted more informal personal photos, such as party pictures, and presented themselves as relaxed, funny and cool on Facebook, compared with those low in that aspect of self-efficacy (Kramer & Winter, 2008).

These findings answer the review question on computer self-efficacy: it is confidence in using computers and the Internet, it differs by gender in some samples, and it shapes how much and in what way we communicate, explore and present ourselves online.
sections.simple: Internet self-efficacy is confidence in using the Internet well. In Taiwan, girls were more confident communicating online and boys exploring; in the US, men had higher computer self-efficacy. Socially confident Turkish students were more likely to get addicted to the Internet, and Germans confident about making a good impression posted more casual, fun Facebook photos.
keyPoints: Internet self-efficacy: confidence in using the Internet effectively.
Taiwan 8th graders: no overall gender difference; girls confident communicating, boys exploring (Tsai & Tsai, 2010).
US college men higher in computer self-efficacy than women (Buse, 2010).
High social self-efficacy linked to self-esteem but also Internet addiction (Iskender & Akin, 2010).
Impression-management self-efficacy: more informal, relaxed Facebook self-presentation (Kramer & Winter, 2008).

sections.heading: The Relationship between Aggressive Behavior and Televised and Online Violence
sections.detailed:
Bandura and researchers in many countries have shown convincingly that, in the laboratory and in the real world, seeing violence begets violence, whether on television or computer screens, in movies and video games, or in homes, streets and schools (Elson & Ferguson, 2014). The evidence is strong enough that the U.S. Surgeon General, the National Institute of Mental Health, the American Psychological Association, the American Medical Association and the American Psychiatric Association agree that exposure to violence is a significant risk factor for violence in those who witness it (Pozios, Kamban, & Bender, 2013).

Television. A large literature review confirmed the link between watching violent TV in childhood and later aggression (Rogoff, Paradise, Arauz, Correa-Chavez, & Angelillo, 2003). People in their early and mid-20s showed a strong positive correlation between the amount of TV violence watched between ages 6 and 10 and their aggression as adults: the more TV violence in childhood, the more aggressive in their 20s (Huesmann, Moise-Titus, Podolski, & Eron, 2003). German teenagers' exposure to media violence was highly related to aggression (Krahe, Busching, & Moller, 2012).

Short-term effects. Researchers also examined aggressive acts shortly after people viewed televised violence. One analysis found a brief but sharp rise in violent actions peaking three to four days after highly publicised riots (Phillips, 1985). US murder rates rose more than 12 percent above the expected rate in the three days after a televised championship boxing match, a pattern maintained over 15 years (Phillips, 1983). Self-directed violence also increases: suicides tend to climb after the suicide of a movie star or other celebrity (Phillips, 1974).

Video games. Research on large samples of children, teenagers and college students in the United States, Japan and other countries showed that playing violent video games increased aggressive and hostile behavior and led to more drinking and drug use than among non-players. Violent-game players were more likely to get into fights, argue with teachers and do poorly in school, were less likely to help others, and had higher cardiovascular arousal. In general, the more violent the games, the more violent the resulting behavior (Anderson et al., 2010; Bartholow, Sestir, & Davis, 2005; Gentile, Lynch, Linder, & Walsh, 2004; Holtz & Appel, 2011; Huesmann, 2010; Krahe & Moller, 2004; Padilla-Walker, Nelson, Carroll, & Jensen, 2010; Uhlmann & Swanson, 2004).

Cyberbullying. Studies in the United States, Canada and Spain found that having a computer without parental control or monitoring can lead to high online aggression, including cyberbullying, among boys and girls aged 12 to 17 (Calvete et al., 2010; Law, Shapka, & Olson, 2010; Werner & Bumpus, 2010). People high in self-efficacy and self-esteem are much less bothered by being cyberbullied (Raskauskas, Rubiano, Offen, & Wayland, 2015). Those high in disinhibition, whose moral restraints are weakened by watching a model do harm, are much more given to cyberbullying (Bussey, Fitzpatrick, & Raman, 2015; Udris, 2014).
sections.simple: Seeing violence leads to violence, and major US health and psychology bodies agree it's a real risk factor. Kids who watched more TV violence at 6-10 were more aggressive in their 20s; murders rose after televised boxing matches, and suicides after celebrity suicides. Violent video games raise aggression, and unmonitored computer use plus disinhibition feeds cyberbullying.
keyPoints: Seeing violence begets violence; major US health and psychology bodies call it a significant risk factor.
TV violence at ages 6-10 predicted aggression in the 20s (Huesmann et al., 2003).
Phillips: violence peaked 3-4 days after riots; murders up 12% after boxing; suicides after celebrity suicides.
Violent video games: more aggression, hostility, drinking, drug use, fights, poorer school work, less helping, higher arousal.
More violent games, more violent behavior.
Cyberbullying: linked to unmonitored computers and disinhibition; high self-efficacy buffers victims.

sections.heading: Reflections on Bandura's Theory
sections.detailed:
Criticisms. Social-learning theory focuses on overt behavior, and critics argue that this ignores distinctly human inner aspects of personality such as motivation and emotion. They use the analogy of a physician whose patients have stomach pains: a doctor who deals only with overt behavior might simply tell patients to stop groaning, complaining and clutching their stomachs, when what is needed is medication or surgery to treat the diseased internal organ. If only the symptom is treated and not the cause, critics say, substitute symptoms may appear. The chapter summary adds two further criticisms: the theory excludes emotions and conflicts, and Bandura failed to state precisely how cognitive variables affect behavior.

Advantages. First, the approach is objective and suited to laboratory methods, which fits the emphasis of experimental psychology. Most experimental psychologists reject personality theories built on unconscious or other internal forces that cannot be manipulated or measured in the lab. Bandura's approach therefore has a great deal of empirical support, especially the concept of self-efficacy, whose usefulness continues to be confirmed in the lab and in real-world settings.

Second, observational learning and behavior modification fit the functional, pragmatic spirit of American psychology. More readily than other approaches, these techniques can be taken from the lab and applied to practical problems. They also give the practitioner more immediate reinforcement: in clinical settings, dramatic changes in client behavior can be seen within weeks or even days.

Overall evaluation. Despite the criticisms about inner experience and symptom-focused treatment, social-learning theory and the successful use of modeling to change behavior remain extremely popular. The many books, articles and studies still flowing from the theory attest to its continuing appeal as a way to study behavior in the lab and change it in the real world.
sections.simple: Critics say Bandura focuses too much on visible behavior and ignores emotions, motivation and inner conflicts, like a doctor treating only the groaning and not the sick organ. He also never said exactly how thoughts affect behavior. But his theory is objective, testable, strongly supported (especially self-efficacy) and practical, producing quick real-world change.
keyPoints: Criticism: focus on overt behavior ignores motivation, emotion and conflicts.
Stomach-pain analogy: treating symptoms, not causes, may produce substitute symptoms.
Criticism: no precise account of how cognitive variables affect behavior.
Strength: objective, lab-testable, strong empirical support, especially for self-efficacy.
Strength: pragmatic and applicable; quick clinical change within weeks or days.
Theory remains extremely popular.

sections.heading: The Widespread Use of Role Models
sections.detailed:
Behavioral change based on Bandura's ideas has been demonstrated on a large scale in some 60 nations. His central idea, that people learn behaviors from role models they wish to emulate, has been used in radio and television programs in less well-developed nations to promote social issues such as population control, improving the status of women and reducing the spread of AIDS (Kaufman, Cornish, Zimmerman, & Johnson, 2014).

The stories in these programs revolve around characters who model behaviors designed to achieve public health goals, both for themselves and for society. Studies have shown significant changes in safe-sex practices and family planning among millions of people after exposure to these models, supporting the idea that Bandura's ideas can be applied to national as well as individual problems (Smith, 2002).

It is therefore not surprising that many researchers and clinicians continue to study and promote social-learning theory. The large number of books, articles and research studies still derived from it shows its continuing popularity both for studying behavior in the laboratory and for modifying behavior in the real world.

This is a strong concluding point for long answers: the same mechanism shown with a Bobo doll in a lab has been scaled up through mass media to change health behavior across whole societies.
sections.simple: Bandura's idea that people copy role models has been used in radio and TV dramas in about 60 countries. Characters modeled healthy behavior like family planning and safe sex, and millions of viewers changed their behavior. This shows his ideas work for whole nations, not just individuals.
keyPoints: Large-scale behavior change shown in some 60 nations.
Radio and TV dramas used role models to promote population control, women's status and AIDS prevention (Kaufman et al., 2014).
Millions changed safe-sex and family-planning practices (Smith, 2002).
Bandura's ideas apply to national as well as individual problems.
Continued research output shows the theory's lasting popularity.

terms.definition: Bandura's approach that studies how behavior is formed and modified in a social context, among people interacting with each other.
Learning new responses by watching how other people behave.
Learning or strengthening a behavior by observing others' behavior and its consequences, rather than experiencing the reinforcement directly.
Thought processes that sit between stimulus and response, letting us anticipate consequences and consciously decide whether to imitate.
Observing a model's behavior and repeating it; as a behavior-modification technique, observing models and participating with them in performing the desired behavior.
An inflatable plastic figure about 4 feet tall used in Bandura's classic studies of children imitating an aggressive model.
Inducing behavior through full verbal explanation or instruction, usually supplemented by behavioral demonstration.
The weakening of inhibitions or constraints by observing the behavior of a model.
An online form of disinhibition: posting inflammatory, derogatory or hateful messages about a person or group, aided by crowd-like anonymity.
The three factors that influence modeling: characteristics of the models, characteristics of the observers, and reward consequences of the behavior.
The first process of observational learning: perceiving the model accurately enough, and paying enough attention, to acquire the information needed to imitate.
Remembering the model's behavior by encoding it symbolically in imaginal and verbal form so it can be repeated later.
Retaining a model's behavior as vivid, easily retrievable mental pictures used later as a basis for imitation.
Retaining a model's behavior by describing it to oneself in words; these codes can be silently rehearsed and later serve as cues.
Translating symbolic representations of a model's behavior into overt behavior; essentially practice with feedback on accuracy.
Perceiving that the model's behavior is rewarded and expecting similar consequences, which motivates performance and also boosts attention and retention.
Not a psychic agent that causes behavior but a set of cognitive processes and structures concerned with thought and perception.
Administering rewards or punishments to oneself for meeting, exceeding or falling short of one's own expectations or standards.
Subjective criteria or reference points, first learned from models, against which we evaluate our own behavior in self-reinforcement.
Our feeling of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life; also our perception of control over our lives.
The most influential source of self-efficacy information: our own previous successes and failures, including feedback on performance.
A source of self-efficacy information: seeing others, especially similar others, succeed (raises it) or fail (lowers it).
A source of self-efficacy information: being reminded that one has the ability to succeed; probably the most common source, effective only if realistic.
A source of self-efficacy information: how calm or anxious we feel in a stressful situation; higher arousal means lower self-efficacy.
Changing learned behaviors that society considers undesirable by targeting the behavior or symptom itself rather than presumed unconscious conflicts.
A behavior-therapy technique in which a person watches a live model and then participates with the model in the feared activity.
A behavior-therapy technique in which a person imagines a model coping with a feared or threatening situation without actually seeing one.
The idea that behavior is controlled by the individual, through cognitive processes, and by the environment, through external social stimulus events.
The level of our belief about how good our memory is; low memory self-efficacy can impair performance on memory tests.
Parents' belief that they are effective parents; high levels are linked to higher self-efficacy and fewer problems in their children.
Having a round face, large eyes, small nose bridge and small chin; linked to low control beliefs in young and middle adulthood.
A group's shared sense, when working together toward specific goals, that it can overcome obstacles and achieve those goals.
Our feelings of confidence in our ability to use the Internet effectively.
Confidence in one's ability to initiate social contact and make new friends easily.
Online aggression toward others; linked to unmonitored computer use and to disinhibition.

people.name: Albert Bandura
people.contribution: Developed social-learning (observational-learning) theory, the Bobo doll studies, the four processes of observational learning, self-efficacy, reciprocal determinism and modeling-based behavior therapy.

people.name: B. F. Skinner
people.contribution: Bandura agreed with him that behavior is learned but rejected his focus on animal subjects, direct reinforcement only, and a direct stimulus-response link without cognition.

people.name: Bandura, Ross, & Ross
people.contribution: Classic 1963 Bobo doll study: children who saw an aggressive model were twice as aggressive as controls.

people.name: Walters
people.contribution: Co-researched the 1963 study on parents of aggressive and inhibited children with Bandura, and the 1963 eye-movement disinhibition study (Walters, Bowen, & Parke).

people.name: Maddux
people.contribution: Described self-efficacy as the power of believing you can, a key ingredient in success (2002).

people.name: Alfred Adler
people.contribution: Like Adler, Bandura considered birth order important; high self-efficacy has been linked to Adler's characteristics of mental health such as social interest.

people.name: Schneewind
people.contribution: Found that parental behaviors producing high self-efficacy differ for boys and girls (1995).

people.name: Bandura, Blanchard, & Ritter
people.contribution: Classic 1969 snake-phobia study using filmed models making progressively closer contact with snakes.

people.name: Melamed & Siegel
people.contribution: Showed a hospital-coping film reduced anxiety and later behavior problems in children facing surgery (1975).

people.name: Sarason
people.contribution: Showed a model describing coping mechanisms improved recall in high test-anxiety students (1975).

people.name: Hackett
people.contribution: Found women feel low self-efficacy for traditionally male careers despite comparable measured abilities (1995).

people.name: Stajkovic & Luthans
people.contribution: Meta-analysis of 114 studies linking higher self-efficacy to better job performance (1998).

people.name: Huesmann
people.contribution: With colleagues, linked childhood TV violence (ages 6-10) to adult aggression (2003); also cited on violent video games (2010).

people.name: Phillips
people.contribution: Documented short-term rises in violence after publicised riots, murders after televised boxing, and suicides after celebrity suicides (1974, 1983, 1985).

people.name: Jerusalem & Mittag
people.contribution: Found highly self-efficacious East German migrants coped better with migration stress (1995).

people.name: Watson, Chemers, & Preiser
people.contribution: Showed collective efficacy in college basketball teams predicted end-of-season standings (2001).

studies.title: Bandura, Ross, & Ross (1963): Bobo doll
studies.finding: Preschoolers who saw an adult attack Bobo were twice as aggressive as controls; aggression was equally intense whether the model was live, televised or a cartoon.

studies.title: Bandura & Walters (1963): parents of aggressive and inhibited children
studies.finding: Inhibited children had inhibited parents and aggressive children had aggressive parents, showing modeling of parental behavior.

studies.title: Walters, Bowen, & Parke (1963): disinhibition of perceptual responses
studies.finding: Male students copied a supposed model's eye movements over erotic pictures; modeling shaped what they looked at and perceived.

studies.title: Zhuo (2010): trolling
studies.finding: Some adolescents have been driven to suicide by cruel, widespread online comments directed at them by name.

studies.title: Thacker & Griffiths (2012): trolling among gamers
studies.finding: Frequent video gamers most into trolling were younger and male; motives included revenge, boredom and amusement.

studies.title: Vaidya, Latzman, Markon, & Watson (2010): disinhibition and age
studies.finding: Disinhibition was strong among 18- to 19-year-olds but greatly reduced among 22- to 25-year-olds.

studies.title: Bandura: similarity of model
studies.finding: Children imitated a live child, a filmed child and a cartoon, but imitation fell as similarity decreased; even cartoons beat no-model controls.

studies.title: Pedestrian red-light crossing
studies.finding: Pedestrians crossed against a red light more often when a well-dressed rather than poorly dressed person crossed.

studies.title: Esseilly, Rat-Fischer, O'Regan, & Fagard (2013): infants and tools
studies.finding: Infants as young as 16 months imitated a model using a rake to get a toy, but only if first shown the tool's purpose.

studies.title: Kuhn & Kinsky (2013): caregiver models
studies.finding: College students who had observed a positive caregiver-child relationship modeled it in their romantic relationships.

studies.title: Leatherdale & Papadakis (2011): weight of models
studies.finding: Canadian 9th and 10th graders at schools where older students were overweight gained more weight.

studies.title: Bandura (1965): model rewarded vs punished
studies.finding: Children who saw the Bobo-hitting model punished were significantly less aggressive than those who saw the model rewarded with praise, soda and candy.

studies.title: Bandura: TV and video-game models without reward
studies.finding: Children imitated a model on TV or in a video game regardless of whether they were promised a reward.

examples.title: Vicarious reinforcement: the late submission
examples.text: A student sees a classmate lose marks for submitting an assignment late. Without ever being penalised himself, he starts submitting on time. He learned from the consequence someone else received.

examples.title: Disinhibition: comment-section pile-on
examples.text: Someone who would never insult a person face to face joins a flood of nasty replies under an influencer's post after seeing dozens of others do it anonymously. The models and the crowd-like anonymity weaken his usual restraint.

examples.title: Four processes: learning to make a reel
examples.text: You watch a creator's editing tutorial closely (attention), save notes and remember the shot sequence (retention), try editing your own clip and fix mistakes after friends comment (production), and keep going because you saw the creator's reel go viral (motivation).

examples.title: Sources of self-efficacy before a viva
examples.text: A PG student feels more confident for a viva after doing well in a mock viva (performance attainment), watching a senior from a similar background pass (vicarious experience), hearing a guide say she is ready (verbal persuasion), and practising slow breathing so she feels calm (physiological arousal).

examples.title: Covert modeling for stage fear
examples.text: A student afraid of speaking at a college fest is asked to imagine a peer walking up nervously, taking a breath and delivering the talk well. Without seeing a real model, the imagined coping reduces her fear.

examples.title: Collective efficacy in a cricket team
examples.text: A college cricket team that won most matches last season and has a confident captain starts the new season believing it can beat anyone. That shared belief helps it hold together under pressure in close games.
