practice.q: Define vicarious reinforcement.
practice.answer: Vicarious reinforcement is learning or strengthening a behavior by watching other people's behavior and the consequences it brings them, instead of experiencing the reinforcement directly. It is the distinctive feature of Bandura's observational-learning approach: we can learn what to do, and what to avoid, from what happens to others.

practice.q: What is disinhibition?
practice.answer: Disinhibition is the weakening of inhibitions or restraints through observing a model. Behaviors a person normally suppresses are performed more readily when others are seen doing them, as when people in a crowd riot or anonymous users post hateful comments online (trolling).

practice.q: What does Bandura mean by self-efficacy? Give an example of how it helps us control our lives.
practice.answer: Self-efficacy is our feeling of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life, or our perceived control over life events. For example, a student who believes she can master statistics keeps working through early failures and treats a low score as a challenge, which makes eventual success more likely.

practice.q: What is reciprocal determinism?
practice.answer: Reciprocal determinism is Bandura's view that behavior is controlled both by the person, through cognitive processes, and by the environment, through external social stimulus events. People are neither powerless objects of the environment nor completely free agents; person and environment determine each other.

practice.q: What is collective efficacy?
practice.answer: Collective efficacy is the shared sense, in a group working together toward specific goals, that it can overcome obstacles and achieve those goals. Examples are a sports team, an organizational department, a combat unit or neighbors uniting against drug dealers.

practice.q: What is computer (Internet) self-efficacy? How might it influence online behavior?
practice.answer: It is our confidence in our ability to use computers and the Internet effectively. It shapes online behavior: for example, Taiwanese girls were more confident communicating online and boys exploring, and people confident in making a good impression presented themselves more informally on Facebook.

practice.q: How does Bandura deal with internal cognitive processes and with the unconscious?
practice.answer:
Unlike Skinner, Bandura gave cognitive processes a central place. He argued that we do not imitate automatically; we make a deliberate, conscious decision to behave like a model. To learn through example and vicarious reinforcement we must anticipate and appreciate the consequences of what we observe. By imagining these consequences we can regulate our behavior even without experiencing them. So there is no direct link between stimulus and response, or behavior and reinforcer; cognitive processes mediate between them (p. 342).

Cognition also appears in retention (imaginal and verbal representational systems), in incentive processes (anticipating reinforcement), and in the self, which Bandura defines as a set of cognitive processes and structures concerned with thought and perception. Self-reinforcement and self-efficacy are cognitive aspects of the self (pp. 349-351).

The unconscious, by contrast, plays no role. Bandura did not try to deal with supposed underlying unconscious conflicts in therapy; the target was the behavior or symptom, not a presumed internal neurosis (pp. 354-355). He also avoided free association, dream analysis and projective techniques, assessing instead observable behavior and measurable cognitive variables (p. 357).

In short, Bandura accepts conscious cognition as a mediator of behavior but ignores the unconscious.

practice.q: What is Bandura's position on the role of reinforcement in learning?
practice.answer:
Bandura agreed with Skinner that much learning occurs through reinforcement, but he rejected the idea that behavior can be learned or changed only through direct reinforcement (pp. 342-343).

First, reinforcement can be vicarious. By observing others' behavior and its consequences, we learn without being reinforced ourselves (p. 342). Seeing a model rewarded makes us more likely to imitate, while seeing a model punished reduces imitation, as in the Bobo doll study where children who saw the model punished were less aggressive (Bandura, 1965, p. 348).

Second, reinforcement works mainly through anticipation. Seeing a model's behavior rewarded leads us to expect similar consequences, which motivates us to attend, remember and perform correctly (p. 350).

Third, reinforcement is not always necessary. Loud sounds, bright lights and exciting videos capture attention without reinforcement, and children imitate TV and video-game models whether or not they are promised a reward. Reinforcement assists modeling but is not vital (p. 350).

Fourth, reinforcement can come from three sources: another person, vicarious experience or oneself. Self-reinforcement becomes especially important for older children and adults (pp. 350-351).

Thus for Bandura reinforcement facilitates learning but observation and cognition are central.

practice.q: Describe a typical experiment in which modeling is used to change behavior.
practice.answer:
A classic example is the snake-phobia study by Bandura, Blanchard and Ritter (1969). Adults with an intense fear of snakes watched a film in which children, adolescents and adults made progressively closer contact with a snake. The filmed models first handled plastic snakes, then touched live snakes, and finally let a large snake crawl over their bodies. The phobic participants could stop the film whenever scenes became too threatening. Gradually their fear of snakes was overcome (p. 355).

A similar earlier study (Bandura, Grusec, & Menlove, 1967) used children afraid of dogs. From a safe distance they watched a same-age child make progressively bolder moves toward a dog, petting it through a playpen and then playing with it inside. Their fear was considerably reduced (p. 355).

These experiments show the key features of modeling therapy: a model similar to the observer, graduated exposure from mild to more threatening steps, observer control over pace, and comparison with untreated conditions. The logic is that if behaviors are learned by modeling, they can be relearned the same way. Benefits extended beyond the phobia itself: one woman could wear a necklace for the first time and a realtor earned more because he could visit rural properties (p. 355).

practice.q: Explain disinhibition. How can it explain both mob behavior and online trolling?
practice.answer:
Disinhibition is the weakening of an inhibition or restraint through exposure to a model (Bandura, 1973, 1986). Behaviors people normally suppress are performed more readily when they see a model perform them (p. 345).

Mob behavior. In a crowd, people may riot, breaking windows and shouting, doing things they would never do alone. Seeing others around them act aggressively makes them drop their own inhibitions against aggression.

Trolling. Posting comments online after others' example gives the same anonymity as being in a large crowd. This leads to trolling, posting inflammatory, derogatory or hateful messages about a person or group. Some adolescents have been driven to suicide by such comments (Zhuo, 2010). Among frequent gamers, trollers were younger and male and trolled for revenge, boredom or amusement (Thacker & Griffiths, 2012).

The common explanation is that in both cases models plus anonymity weaken normal restraints. Disinhibition can also affect perception, as Walters, Bowen and Parke (1963) showed: students copied a supposed model's eye movements over erotic pictures. Encouragingly, disinhibition declines with age, being strong at 18-19 and much reduced at 22-25 (Vaidya et al., 2010).

practice.q: Explain how the production processes can be used to teach a person to play tennis.
practice.answer:
Production processes translate the imaginal and verbal representations of a model's behavior into overt behavior; the chapter describes them simply as practice (p. 349). Even after attending to and retaining a behavior, a learner may not perform it correctly, especially highly skilled actions with many component behaviors (p. 350).

Applied to tennis: the learner first watches a coach demonstrate a serve (attention) and stores images and verbal cues such as the toss, the knee bend and the follow-through (retention). On the court, the first attempts will be clumsy, just as the chapter's new driver brakes too early or oversteers. The learner must physically practise the serve repeatedly. The coach provides feedback on the accuracy of each attempt, for example that the toss is too far forward, and the learner adjusts. Through repeated practice with feedback, the separate components are integrated into a smooth, accurate serve (p. 350).

Table 13.1 describes production as physically producing the responses and receiving feedback on continued practice (p. 349). Incentives also matter, since expecting rewards such as winning matches motivates continued practice (p. 350). (The tennis application is an illustration; the chapter's own example is driving.)

practice.q: How do the types of behavior we acquire through modeling change with age?
practice.answer:
Modeling changes with the observer's age in two ways (pp. 347-348).

Capacity to imitate. In infancy modeling is limited to immediate imitation, because infants have not yet developed the imaginal and verbal representational systems needed to imitate after a delay. The modeled behavior must be repeated several times after the infant's first attempt and must lie within the infant's sensorimotor range. By about age 2, children have enough attentional, retention and production ability to imitate some time after observing (p. 347).

What is reinforcing. The reinforcers that lead us to imitate also change. Younger children are reinforced mainly by physical stimuli such as food, affection or punishment. Older children associate positive physical reinforcers with approval from significant models and unpleasant ones with disapproval. Eventually rewards and punishments become self-administered (p. 348), which links to self-reinforcement in older children and adults (p. 350).

Other age effects: we are more influenced by models our own age (p. 346), and disinhibition by models declines from the late teens to the mid-20s (p. 345). Self-efficacy also changes across life, peaking in middle age (p. 358).

practice.q: What is the self in Bandura's view? How does self-reinforcement operate to change behavior?
practice.answer:
For Bandura the self is not a psychic agent that determines behavior but a set of cognitive processes and structures concerned with thought and perception. Its two important aspects are self-reinforcement and self-efficacy (p. 350).

Self-reinforcement means administering rewards or punishments to oneself for meeting, exceeding or falling short of one's own standards. It is as important as external reinforcement for older children and adults. Rewards may be tangible (buying new gym shoes or a car) or emotional (pride, satisfaction); punishments appear as shame, guilt or depression. It resembles conscience or the superego, but Bandura denied they are the same (pp. 350-351).

How it changes behavior. Self-reinforcement requires internal standards of performance against which we evaluate ourselves. Past behavior becomes a reference point and an incentive to do better. When a level of achievement no longer challenges or satisfies us, we raise the standard; failure may lead us to lower it to a realistic level. This continuing cycle regulates much of our behavior (p. 351).

Standards are first learned from models such as parents and teachers, increasingly also from celebrity blogs and social media. Unrealistic standards from very talented models can lead to repeated failure, worthlessness, depression and even substance abuse (p. 351).

practice.q: How do people high in self-efficacy differ from people low in self-efficacy in their ability to cope with life?
practice.answer:
Self-efficacy is our feeling of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life (p. 351).

Low self-efficacy. Such people feel helpless and unable to control life events, believing their efforts are futile. When they meet obstacles they quickly give up if their first attempt fails. Those extremely low do not even try, convinced nothing will make a difference. Low self-efficacy destroys motivation, lowers aspirations, interferes with cognitive abilities and harms physical health (p. 351).

High self-efficacy. Such people believe they can deal effectively with situations. Expecting to overcome obstacles, they persevere and often perform at a high level. They have more confidence and little self-doubt, view difficulties as challenges rather than threats and actively seek novel situations. High self-efficacy reduces fear of failure, raises aspirations and improves problem solving and analytical thinking (pp. 351-352).

Research support: high self-efficacy people earn better grades, set higher career goals and perform better at work, tolerate pain better and recover faster from illness, drink and smoke less, and experience less depression, test anxiety and job stress (highlights, p. 363). They also cope better with stresses such as migration, abortion and the birth of a first child (p. 362).

practice.q: Describe the guided participation and covert modeling approaches to behavior modification.
practice.answer:
Bandura developed three forms of behavior therapy: modeling, guided participation and covert modeling, used for fears, phobias and anxiety (p. 355).

Guided participation involves watching a live model and then participating with the model. In treating snake phobia, clients first watch through an observation window as a live model handles a snake. They then enter the room and watch at close range. Wearing gloves, they are coaxed into touching the middle of the snake while the model holds the head and tail. Eventually they touch the snake without gloves (p. 355). The method combines observation with graduated, supported personal performance, which also builds performance attainment, the strongest source of self-efficacy (p. 352).

Covert modeling shows that modeling works without an observable model. Clients are instructed to imagine a model coping with a feared or threatening situation; they do not actually see a model. It has been used successfully for snake phobias and social inhibitions (p. 355).

Both techniques target the behavior itself rather than unconscious conflicts (p. 355), and their success is linked to increases in self-efficacy during treatment (p. 356). Clients participate knowingly, which Bandura stressed in answering ethical criticisms (p. 357).

practice.q: Give examples of how modeling can be used to reduce anxiety.
practice.answer:
The chapter gives two kinds of anxiety reduced by modeling: fear of medical treatment and test anxiety (p. 356).

Fear of medical treatment. Melamed and Siegel (1975) studied children scheduled for surgery who had never been in hospital. The experimental group watched a film of a boy who, despite initial anxiety, coped well with doctors and procedures; the control group saw a film of a boy on a trip. The modeling film reduced anxiety, and those children had fewer behavior problems after hospitalization. Similar methods reduce adults' fear of hospitals and dentists. In Allen, Danforth and Drabman (1989), over 80 percent of patients initially refused or quit a very stressful procedure; those who watched a model undergo it and describe coping were more likely to complete it, with less anxiety and shorter stays.

Test anxiety. Sarason (1975) divided students into high and low test anxiety. Some saw a model discuss her test anxiety and coping methods, some saw her discuss anxiety without coping, and some saw her discuss other college activities. On a nonsense-syllable recall test, high-anxiety students who saw the coping model did significantly better than high-anxiety students in the other conditions.

The common lesson is that a coping model who shows some anxiety and then deals with it effectively is especially helpful.

practice.q: What is Bandura's position on free will versus determinism and on heredity versus environment?
practice.answer:
Free will versus determinism. Bandura's position is reciprocal determinism. Behavior is controlled by the person, through cognitive processes, and by the environment, through external social situations (p. 357). He stated that people are neither powerless objects controlled by environmental forces nor free agents who can become whatever they choose; people and environments are reciprocal determinants of each other (1977). This is a middle position: unlike Skinner, he gives the person some control through cognition, self-reinforcement and self-efficacy, but he does not accept unlimited free will.

Heredity versus environment. According to the chapter summary, Bandura held that most behavior is learned and genetic factors play only a minor role (p. 367). His whole theory rests on learning from models, from parents onward (p. 345).

Related positions. Learning in childhood may be more influential than learning in adulthood, but adults are not victims of their childhood experiences (p. 367); behavior can be changed at any age through modeling therapy. Our ultimate goal is to set realistic performance standards to maintain an optimal level of self-efficacy (p. 367). Overall his image of human nature is optimistic and emphasises human capacity for self-regulation and control.

practice.q: How does self-efficacy differ as a function of gender, age and physical attractiveness?
practice.answer:
Gender and age. On average men score higher than women in self-efficacy; this gap peaks in the 20s and then declines. For both sexes self-efficacy increases through childhood and early adulthood, peaks in middle age and declines after 60 (Gecas, 1989; Lachman, 1985; p. 358). Individual differences remain wide: Dutch older adults who believed their memory was declining performed worse six years later (Valentijn et al., 2006), and a review of over 100 studies confirmed that low memory self-efficacy impairs memory performance (Beaudoin & Desrichard, 2011). Gender also affects career self-efficacy: women feel low efficacy for traditionally male jobs despite equal abilities (Hackett, 1995; p. 359).

Physical appearance. Among adults aged 25 to 76, appearance affected feelings of control more than self-esteem or health (Andreoletti, Zebrowitz, & Lachman, 2001). Baby-faceness was related to low control beliefs in young and middle adulthood, but older baby-faced adults reported stronger control, possibly because they looked younger; effects were stronger for women. People rated less attractive reported lower feelings of control in job and social situations, and shorter people reported lower control in young adulthood than taller or average-height people (pp. 358-359).

These findings support Bandura's idea that appearance influences the reinforcers we get from others and thus how we feel about ourselves.

practice.q: In what ways can collective efficacy influence the behavior of group members?
practice.answer:
Collective efficacy is a group's shared belief that, working together, it can overcome obstacles and achieve its goals (Dithurbide & Feltz, 2012; p. 362).

Sports. College basketball teams with competent leaders and many wins the previous season developed high collective efficacy, and teams highest in it at the season's start finished higher in the standings (Watson, Chemers, & Preiser, 2001; pp. 362-363).

Families and schools. High family collective efficacy produced more open communication, more truthful disclosure by teens and greater family satisfaction (Bandura et al., 2011). High teacher collective efficacy in the Netherlands raised student achievement (Moolenaar et al., 2012). Higher collective efficacy among US students reduced bullying (Williams & Guerra, 2011), and Greek classes high in it showed far less bullying (Sapouna, 2010) (p. 363).

Neighborhoods. Even in tough inner-city areas, high collective efficacy is linked to less alcoholism, drug use, violence and crime including murder (p. 363).

Organizations. Collective efficacy increases job performance and helping and reduces workplace stress in Western countries and China; Italian air force units higher in it showed greater commitment and job satisfaction (p. 364).

Thus collective efficacy raises performance, cooperation, openness and satisfaction and lowers antisocial behavior.

practice.q: In what ways does Bandura's observational-learning approach differ from other approaches to personality, especially Skinner's behaviorism and psychoanalysis? Discuss.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Albert Bandura's social-learning or observational-learning theory holds that personality consists largely of learned behavior, but that most of this learning takes place by observing other people in a social context. It differs both from Skinner's radical behaviorism and from psychodynamic approaches.

Differences from Skinner. Bandura agreed with Skinner that behavior is learned, but the similarity ends there (p. 341). First, Bandura criticised Skinner's reliance on individual animal subjects; he argued that data from experiments without social interaction cannot be expected to apply to real life, since few people live in isolation. His research used normal humans in social interaction (pp. 341-342).

Second, Skinner emphasised direct reinforcement of one's own responses. Bandura argued that virtually all behavior can be learned vicariously, by observing others and the consequences they receive (p. 342). Operant trial-and-error is inefficient and even dangerous for skills such as swimming or driving (p. 343). The Bobo doll studies showed children acquiring aggressive responses simply by watching a model (p. 344).

Third, Skinner excluded cognition and proposed a direct stimulus-response link. Bandura held that cognitive processes mediate between stimulus and response: we consciously decide whether to imitate and anticipate consequences before acting (p. 342). Hence his theory is a less extreme behaviorism.

Fourth, reinforcement is not essential: children imitate TV and video-game models without promised reward, and reinforcement may be external, vicarious or self-administered (p. 350). Finally, for Skinner reinforcers control behavior, while for Bandura models control behavior (p. 346).

Differences from psychoanalysis and other internal approaches. Bandura's work is based on rigorous laboratory research rather than on a neurotic person on a couch (p. 342). He ignores the unconscious; therapy targets the behavior or symptom, not a presumed internal neurosis (p. 355). He avoids free association, dream analysis and projective techniques, assessing behavior and cognitive variables through observation, self-report and physiological measures (p. 357). The self is not a psychic agent but a set of cognitive processes (p. 350), and although self-reinforcement resembles the superego, Bandura denies they are the same (p. 351). He also rejects the idea that adults are victims of childhood (p. 367).

Distinctive concepts. The theory adds the four processes of observational learning, disinhibition, self-efficacy, collective efficacy and reciprocal determinism, the view that person and environment determine each other (p. 357). Its methods are experimental, with control groups, large samples and statistics (p. 357).

Conclusion. Bandura's approach thus stands between radical behaviorism and cognitive theories: it keeps the behaviorist emphasis on learning and objective research but adds social observation, cognition and self-regulation. Its practicality and empirical support, especially for self-efficacy, explain its continuing popularity (p. 366), though critics say it neglects emotion, motivation and inner conflict.

practice.q: How does modeling vary as a function of the characteristics of the models, the characteristics of the observers and the reward consequences of the behavior?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Modeling is learning by observing a model and repeating the behavior. Bandura and his associates (Bandura, 1977, 1986) found three factors that influence it: characteristics of the models, characteristics of the observers and the reward consequences associated with the behavior (p. 346).

1. Characteristics of the models. Similarity: we are more influenced by models similar to us. Children imitated a live child, a filmed child and a cartoon, but imitation decreased as similarity decreased; live models were copied more than cartoons, though even cartoons produced more imitation than no model (p. 346). Age and sex: we model more on people of our own sex and age, and successful peers facing the same problems are highly influential. Status: pedestrians crossed against a red light more when a well-dressed person did; advertisers use athletes and celebrities for this reason. Type of behavior: simple behaviors are copied more readily than complex ones, and hostile, aggressive behaviors are strongly imitated, especially by children. Infants of 16 months imitated tool use only when shown its purpose (Esseilly et al., 2013), and students modeled positive caregiver-child relationships in their romances (Kuhn & Kinsky, 2013) (pp. 346-347). Size and weight: Canadian students at schools with overweight older students gained more weight (Leatherdale & Papadakis, 2011; p. 347).

2. Characteristics of the observers. Age: infants can imitate only immediately, since their imaginal and verbal representational systems are undeveloped; the behavior must be repeated and within their sensorimotor range. By about age 2, delayed imitation is possible (p. 347). The reinforcers that matter change with age, from physical stimuli in young children, to approval and disapproval of significant models, to self-administered rewards (p. 348). Attributes: people low in self-confidence and self-esteem imitate more, and those previously reinforced for imitating, such as a child rewarded for copying an older sibling, are more susceptible to models (p. 348).

3. Reward consequences. The rewards linked to a behavior can override both model and observer characteristics. A high-status model may prompt imitation, but if the rewards are not meaningful we stop the behavior and are less influenced by that model later. Seeing the model rewarded or punished also matters: in Bandura's 1965 Bobo doll study, children who saw the model punished were significantly less aggressive than those who saw the model praised and given soda and candy (p. 348).

Conclusion. Modeling is therefore not automatic copying. It depends on who the model is, who the observer is and what consequences follow. These factors also work through the attentional process, since similar, high-status, attractive and expert models draw more attention (p. 348). The analysis explains why advertisers use celebrities, why children copy aggressive media figures, and why therapy uses similar, coping models.

practice.q: What are the four processes of observational learning? How are they related?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Bandura analysed observational learning and found it governed by four related mechanisms: attentional processes, retention processes, production processes, and incentive and motivational processes (Table 13.1, p. 348).

1. Attentional processes. Modeling cannot occur unless the observer attends to the model. Mere exposure does not guarantee attention to relevant cues or accurate perception; the observer must perceive the model accurately enough to gain the information needed (p. 348). Attention is greater for models who are similar in age and sex, high in status, celebrities, experts, confident or attractive; television, YouTube and online models are especially effective. It also depends on the observer's cognitive and perceptual skills and knowledge, on whether the observer expects to perform the behavior, and on whether the behavior produces positive or negative rather than neutral consequences (pp. 348-349). Example: staying awake in driver's education class.

2. Retention processes. We must remember significant aspects of the behavior to repeat it later, which requires encoding and symbolic representation. In the imaginal system we form vivid, easily retrieved images of the model's behavior. In the verbal system we describe the behavior to ourselves; these codes can be silently rehearsed and later provide hints and cues (p. 349). Example: taking notes on a lecture or video about driving.

3. Production processes. These translate symbolic representations into overt behavior, essentially practice. Even well-retained behavior may be performed poorly at first, especially complex skills. A new driver brakes too soon or oversteers; practice of the physical movements with feedback on accuracy is needed for smooth performance (pp. 349-350). Example: practising gear shifts and dodging cones with an instructor.

4. Incentive and motivational processes. Without incentive or motivation, learned behavior will not be performed. Seeing a model rewarded leads us to anticipate similar consequences, which motivates attention, retention and correct performance. However, reinforcement is not always necessary: bright lights or exciting videos capture attention, and children imitate TV and game models without promised rewards. Reinforcement may be given by others, experienced vicariously or self-administered (p. 350). Example: expecting to pass the test and get a license.

How they are related. The processes form a sequence in which each depends on the previous one: we cannot retain what we did not attend to, or produce what we did not retain. But motivation acts throughout: incentives speed the translation of observation into action and also influence attention and retention, because without incentive we attend less, and with less attention there is less to retain (p. 350). Observer characteristics such as age also link them: infants lack the representational systems for retention, and by age 2 attentional, retention and production abilities allow delayed imitation (p. 347).

Conclusion. Observational learning is thus an active, cognitive process, not passive copying. The four-process model explains why exposure to a model does not always produce imitation and guides practical teaching, from driving lessons to therapy.

practice.q: On what sources of information do we base judgments of our self-efficacy? How can self-efficacy be increased?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Self-efficacy is our feeling of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life, and our perceived control over life events (p. 351). Meeting our standards raises it and failing lowers it. Bandura identified four sources of information on which self-efficacy judgments are based (p. 352).

1. Performance attainment. This is the most influential source. Previous successes directly show our mastery and competence and strengthen self-efficacy; prior failures, especially repeated failures in childhood, lower it. Feedback is an important indicator. College students given positive feedback on complicated puzzles reported higher perceived competence than those given negative feedback (Elliot et al., 2000). Older adults who completed six months of Tai Chi reported significant increases in self-efficacy (Li et al., 2001). Female students who completed a 16-hour self-defense course gained self-efficacy in physical competence, coping and assertiveness, while controls showed no change (Weitlauf et al., 2001). The more we achieve, the more we believe we can achieve (p. 352).

2. Vicarious experiences. Seeing others succeed raises self-efficacy, especially if they are similar to us in ability: if they can do it, so can I. Seeing others fail lowers it. Effective models also show strategies for difficult situations (p. 352).

3. Verbal persuasion. Reminding people that they can achieve their goals can raise self-efficacy. It may be the most common source, used by parents, teachers, spouses, coaches, friends and therapists. It must be realistic; encouraging a 5-foot person to play professional basketball is poor advice compared with, say, martial arts (p. 352).

4. Physiological and emotional arousal. How calm or fearful we feel under stress is used to judge coping ability. We feel more able when not agitated, tense or troubled by headaches. The higher our fear, anxiety or tension, the lower our self-efficacy (pp. 352-353).

Increasing self-efficacy. Bandura concluded that self-efficacy can be increased by matching each source (p. 353): (1) arranging reachable goals to provide success experiences and raise performance attainment; (2) exposing people to appropriate models who perform successfully, enhancing vicarious success; (3) providing verbal persuasion that encourages belief in one's ability; and (4) strengthening physiological arousal through proper diet, stress reduction and exercise, which increases strength, stamina and coping ability. He used these methods to help people learn musical instruments, relate better to the opposite sex, master computer skills, quit smoking and conquer phobias and pain (p. 353).

Modeling therapy also raises self-efficacy: as clients' self-efficacy improved during treatment, they coped better with feared objects, and the procedure itself produced the improvement (p. 356). Collective efficacy can similarly grow through competent leadership and past success, as in basketball teams (pp. 362-363).

Conclusion. Self-efficacy is built mainly through real accomplishment, supported by good models, realistic encouragement and a calm, healthy body. Because Bandura saw self-efficacy as the most important factor in success across the life span (p. 354), these sources have wide practical value in education, therapy and health.

practice.q: Describe the developmental changes in self-efficacy from infancy to old age.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Bandura held that self-efficacy develops gradually across the life span and that it is the single most important factor in determining success or failure throughout life (pp. 353-354). He described changes in childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age.

Infancy and childhood. Infants begin to develop self-efficacy as they try to exert greater influence over their physical and social environments. They learn about the consequences of their physical prowess, social skills and language competence, which act on the environment mainly through their effects on parents. Ideally parents respond to the child's activities and communication and provide stimulating surroundings with freedom to explore (p. 353).

Early efficacy experiences centre on parents, and the parental behaviors that build high self-efficacy differ by gender. High self-efficacy men had warm relationships with fathers, while mothers were more demanding; high self-efficacy women experienced pressure from fathers for high achievement (Schneewind, 1995; p. 353).

Parental influence declines as siblings, peers and other adults enter the child's world. Like Adler, Bandura considered birth order important; first-born and only children judge their abilities differently from later-borns. Same-sex siblings compete more than opposite-sex siblings. Successful playmates serve as high-efficacy models and peers provide comparison points (pp. 353-354). Teachers influence self-efficacy through developing cognitive and problem-solving skills, and children often judge their competence by teachers' evaluations. Bandura argued that ability grouping undermines the self-efficacy of lower-group students and grading on a curve dooms poor achievers to low grades (p. 354).

Adolescence. Adolescents face new demands, from growing sexual awareness to choosing a college and career, and must form new competencies and self-appraisals. Success depends largely on self-efficacy built in childhood (p. 354).

Adulthood. Bandura divided adulthood into young adulthood and the middle years. Young adults must adjust to marriage, parenthood and careers; high self-efficacy is needed, and those low in it are likely to fail to adjust. Mothers high in parenting self-efficacy promote it in their children and suffer less despondency and strain (Olioff & Aboud, 1991; Teti & Gelfand, 1991); employed high self-efficacy mothers experience less strain from work-family conflict (Bandura, 1995). The middle years are stressful too, as people reevaluate careers and family and social lives, confront limitations, redefine goals and seek new ways to enhance self-efficacy (p. 354).

Old age. Reassessment is difficult. Declining mental and physical abilities, retirement and social withdrawal force a new self-appraisal. Lower self-efficacy can further impair functioning as a self-fulfilling prophecy; reduced confidence in sexual performance reduces sexual activity, and lower physical efficacy leads to fatigue and less activity. If we no longer believe we can do something, we may stop trying (p. 354).

Research support. Self-efficacy rises through childhood and early adulthood, peaks in middle age and declines after 60, with men higher than women especially in their 20s (Gecas, 1989; Lachman, 1985; p. 358).

Conclusion. Self-efficacy is shaped first by parents and then by siblings, peers and teachers, and each later stage depends on what was built earlier. It can still be increased at any age through success experiences, models, persuasion and physical well-being (p. 353).

practice.q: Discuss the relationship between self-efficacy and physical and mental health.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Self-efficacy, our sense of competence and control in coping with life (p. 351), has been linked by much research to physical well-being and mental health. Bandura noted that efficacy beliefs affect every phase of personal health change (p. 360).

Physical health.
Pain tolerance. Pregnant women taught relaxation and breathing techniques felt more control over childbirth pain; the higher their self-efficacy, the longer they tolerated pain before asking for medication and the less they needed (Manning & Wright, 1983). Among over 15,000 Chinese patients, higher self-efficacy meant less impairment, distress and pain (Jackson et al., 2014). Coping techniques that raise self-efficacy increase endorphins, and low back pain patients higher in self-efficacy reported better functioning and less pain six months after rehabilitation (Altmaier et al., 1993) (p. 360).
Healthy lifestyle. Self-efficacy-enhancing techniques increased physical activity in adults over 60, while low self-efficacy went with sedentary lives (French et al., 2014). Lower self-efficacy was linked to greater alcohol use in Native American and native Alaskan adults (Taylor, 2000), and adolescents higher in self-efficacy resisted peer pressure to smoke (Schwarzer & Fuchs, 1995; Stacy et al., 1992) (p. 361).
Recovery from illness. High self-efficacy patients responded better to treatment for pulmonary disease; heart-attack patients returned to normal activity with less fear and depression when they and their spouses believed in their fitness, and followed exercise programs more (Kaplan et al., 1984; McLeod, 1986). Italian heart patients high in self-efficacy felt less impact of illness (Greco et al., 2015); Israeli diabetics persisted with self-care (Mishali et al., 2011); orthopedic surgery patients did better in rehabilitation (Waldrop et al., 2001); breast cancer patients expecting to stay cancer-free adjusted better (Carver et al., 2000) (p. 361).

Mental health.
Depression and anxiety. Italian children low in social and academic efficacy were more likely to be depressed, and low social efficacy related to depression in US adolescents (Bandura et al., 1999). Dutch adolescents low in social efficacy showed more anxiety, neuroticism and depression (Muris, 2002). In China and Nigeria, high self-efficacy meant less job stress and test anxiety (Li, 2010; Onyeizugbo, 2010). In adults, low social efficacy contributed to depression by hindering social support (Holahan & Holahan, 1987). The relation may be circular, since depression also lowers self-efficacy (Bandura, 1997) (p. 361).
Social interest and self-esteem. High self-efficacy students scored higher in Adler's social interest, striving for perfection and belonging (Dinter, 2000), and in several countries high self-efficacy went with high self-esteem and less procrastination (p. 362).
Coping with stress. Self-efficacy reduces vulnerability to stress and depression, strengthens the immune system, lowers stress hormones and reduces respiratory infections. High self-efficacy helped women cope with abortion (Cozzarelli, 1993) and a first birth (Ozer, 1995), East German migrants adapt after 1990 (Jerusalem & Mittag, 1995), and facially disfigured cancer patients handle rejection (Hagedoorn & Molleman, 2006) (p. 362).

Conclusion. The evidence consistently shows that people high in self-efficacy are healthier, tolerate pain better, recover faster, avoid harmful habits and are less depressed and anxious. Much of the evidence is correlational and possibly circular, but it strongly supports Bandura's view that belief in our abilities influences actual outcomes.

practice.q: How does self-efficacy influence performance in school and on the job, and our ability to cope with stress?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Bandura saw self-efficacy as the most important factor in success or failure throughout life (p. 354). Research in schools, workplaces and stressful life situations supports this.

School performance. There is a significant positive relationship between self-efficacy and academic performance. Teachers high in self-efficacy create more opportunities for students to achieve, and students' self-efficacy is positively related to motivation, effort, aspiration and persistence (Bassi et al., 2007; Gibson & Dembo, 1984; Multon et al., 1991; Zimmerman, 1995). German teachers high in self-efficacy were rated by students as more effective, and positive student ratings raised teachers' self-efficacy further (Holzberger et al., 2013). Bandura (1997) found high-achieving schools had principals focused on education and teachers with high standards, while low-achieving schools had administrator-disciplinarian principals and low expectations. Culture matters: children in collectivist East Germany had lower academic self-efficacy than West German children (Oettingen & Maier, 1999), and Iranian students with stronger ethnic identity had higher self-efficacy (Hejazi & Hasany, 2014) (p. 359). Collective efficacy among teachers raised grades and among students reduced bullying (p. 363). Parental self-efficacy also predicts children's school performance (Steca et al., 2011; p. 358).

Job performance and career. Women feel low self-efficacy for traditionally male occupations despite abilities equal to men's (Hackett, 1995). High self-efficacy employees set higher goals, are more committed and focus on problem solving, while low self-efficacy employees dwell on deficiencies and fear of failure (Locke & Latham, 1990); failure at a computer task lowers self-efficacy (Hardy, 2014). A meta-analysis of 114 studies found higher self-efficacy meant better job performance (Stajkovic & Luthans, 1998), especially for low-complexity jobs (Judge et al., 2007). High self-efficacy workers are more engaged and less burned out (Ventura et al., 2015), perform better with feedback (Schmidt & DeShon, 2010), succeed more in training and report more satisfaction and commitment (pp. 359-360). Organizational collective efficacy also improves performance and reduces stress (p. 364).

Coping with stress. Self-efficacy and a sense of control help people cope with stress and limit its biological harm. Bandura (2001) wrote that coping efficacy reduces vulnerability to stress and depression and strengthens resilience. High self-efficacy is associated with stronger immunity, lower stress hormones and fewer respiratory infections. Women high in self-efficacy coped better with abortion (Cozzarelli, 1993) and a first child (Ozer, 1995). East German migrants high in self-efficacy saw new demands as challenges, with less anxiety and better health (Jerusalem & Mittag, 1995). Disfigured head and neck cancer patients high in self-efficacy experienced less stress from rejection (Hagedoorn & Molleman, 2006) (p. 362).

Conclusion. Across classrooms, workplaces and crises, people who believe they can succeed set higher goals, persist longer, interpret difficulties as challenges and suffer less stress. These findings support Bandura's practical recommendations for raising self-efficacy through success experiences, models, persuasion and physical well-being (p. 353).

practice.q: Describe how exposure to televised, online and video-game violence affects behavior, with reference to Bandura's theory and research.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Bandura's modeling theory predicts that people, especially children, imitate the aggressive behavior they observe. He openly criticised societies that offer violent models through television, movies and video games (pp. 345-346). Research in many countries supports his view.

Theoretical background. In the Bobo doll study, children who watched an adult attack an inflatable doll were twice as aggressive as controls, and the intensity was the same whether the model was live, on television or a cartoon (Bandura, Ross, & Ross, 1963; p. 344). Hostile and aggressive behaviors are strongly imitated by children (p. 346), and children imitate TV and video-game models even without promised reward (p. 350). If we become what we see, the gap between watching an aggressive cartoon and committing violence is small (p. 346). Disinhibition also explains how models weaken restraints against aggression (p. 345).

General evidence. Seeing violence begets violence in the lab and the real world, on screens and in homes, streets and schools (Elson & Ferguson, 2014). The U.S. Surgeon General, NIMH, APA, AMA and American Psychiatric Association agree exposure to violence is a significant risk factor (Pozios et al., 2013; p. 364).

Television. A large review confirmed the link between childhood TV violence and later aggression (Rogoff et al., 2003). People in their 20s showed a strong positive correlation between TV violence watched at ages 6 to 10 and adult aggression (Huesmann et al., 2003). German teenagers' media violence exposure was highly related to aggression (Krahe et al., 2012) (p. 364).

Short-term effects. Violence rose sharply, peaking three to four days after publicised riots (Phillips, 1985). US murder rates rose over 12 percent above expected for three days after televised championship boxing matches, across 15 years (Phillips, 1983). Suicides increased after celebrity suicides (Phillips, 1974) (p. 365).

Video games. Large samples in the US, Japan and elsewhere showed that violent video games increased aggressive and hostile behavior, drinking and drug use; players were more likely to fight, argue with teachers and do poorly in school, less likely to help others, and had higher cardiovascular arousal. The more violent the games, the more violent the behavior (Anderson et al., 2010; Gentile et al., 2004; Huesmann, 2010; and others; p. 365).

Online aggression. Computers without parental control or monitoring led to high online aggression and cyberbullying among 12- to 17-year-olds in the US, Canada and Spain. People high in disinhibition were more given to cyberbullying, while victims high in self-efficacy and self-esteem were less bothered (p. 365). Trolling is itself an online form of disinhibition (p. 345).

Conclusion. Bandura's theory and the research it inspired show that violent models on television, online and in games increase aggressive behavior in children, teens and young adults, both in the short and long term. The practical implications include monitoring children's media use and providing positive models, the same mechanism that has been used to promote healthy behavior through media role models in some 60 nations (p. 366).

practice.q: Critically evaluate Bandura's social-learning theory.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Bandura's social-learning theory explains personality as behavior learned largely by observing models, mediated by cognitive processes and regulated through self-reinforcement and self-efficacy. Its value is best judged by weighing its criticisms against its strengths.

Criticisms.
1. Neglect of inner experience. Social-learning theory focuses on overt behavior, and critics charge that it ignores distinctly human inner aspects such as motivation and emotion (p. 366). The summary adds that it excludes emotions and conflicts (p. 367).
2. Treating symptoms, not causes. Critics compare Bandura to a physician who tells stomach-pain patients to stop groaning instead of treating the diseased organ; if only symptoms are treated, substitute symptoms may appear (p. 366). Bandura's therapy indeed targets the behavior, not presumed unconscious conflict (p. 355).
3. Vague cognition. Although cognitive variables are central, Bandura failed to state precisely how they affect behavior (p. 367).
4. Ethical concerns. Some educators, politicians and psychologists argued behavior modification manipulates people against their will. Bandura replied that it requires client awareness and self-regulation, that clients choose what to change, and that it increases freedom by removing phobic and compulsive constraints (pp. 356-357).

Strengths.
1. Scientific rigor. The approach is objective and suited to lab methods, using experimental and control groups, precise measurement, large samples and statistics (p. 357). It therefore has a great deal of empirical support, particularly for self-efficacy, whose usefulness is confirmed in the lab and real world (p. 366).
2. Practical application. Observational learning and behavior modification fit the pragmatic spirit of American psychology. Techniques move easily from lab to practice and produce dramatic changes within weeks or days (p. 366). Modeling, guided participation and covert modeling have treated phobias, obsessive-compulsive disorder, sexual dysfunction, medical fears and test anxiety, with effects lasting years (pp. 355-356).
3. Broad research impact. Self-efficacy has been linked to school and job performance, health, mental health and coping with stress, and the concept extended to collective and Internet efficacy (pp. 358-365). The theory also illuminated the effects of media and video-game violence (pp. 364-365).
4. Large-scale social use. Role-model dramas in some 60 nations changed safe-sex and family-planning practices among millions (pp. 366-367).
5. Balanced view of human nature. Reciprocal determinism avoids both strict environmental control and unlimited free will (p. 357), and the theory holds that adults are not victims of childhood (p. 367).

Conclusion. Bandura's theory is less complete as an account of emotion, conflict and the inner life, and its cognitive mechanisms are underspecified. But it is among the most empirically supported and practically useful personality theories, as shown by the continuing flow of research and its popularity for studying and modifying behavior (p. 367).

summary: Bandura agreed with Skinner that behavior is learned but argued it is mostly learned socially, by observing others rather than only through direct reinforcement.
Vicarious reinforcement, learning from the consequences others receive, is the distinctive feature of his observational-learning approach.
Cognitive processes mediate between stimulus and response, making his theory a less extreme form of behaviorism based on lab research with normal people.
In the Bobo doll study, children who saw an aggressive model were twice as aggressive as controls, whether the model was live, televised or a cartoon.
Disinhibition is the weakening of restraints by observing a model; it explains mob behavior and online trolling, and declines from the late teens to the mid-20s.
Modeling depends on characteristics of the model (similarity, sex, age, status, type of behavior), the observer (age, self-esteem, past reinforcement) and reward consequences.
Observational learning runs through four related processes: attentional, retention (imaginal and verbal systems), production (practice with feedback) and incentive/motivational.
Reinforcement helps learning but is not essential; it can be external, vicarious or self-administered.
The self is a set of cognitive processes; self-reinforcement against internal standards regulates behavior, and unrealistic standards can lead to depression.
Self-efficacy is the feeling of competence and control in coping with life; high self-efficacy brings perseverance and achievement, low self-efficacy helplessness.
Self-efficacy is judged from performance attainment (strongest), vicarious experience, verbal persuasion and physiological arousal, and can be raised through each.
Self-efficacy develops from infancy (parents) through siblings, peers and teachers, adolescence, adulthood and old age; Bandura saw it as the most important factor in life success.
Modeling, guided participation and covert modeling successfully treat phobias and anxiety; they are efficient, durable and raise self-efficacy.
Bandura rejected ethical charges of manipulation, arguing behavior modification requires awareness, is chosen by clients and increases freedom.
His view of human nature is reciprocal determinism: person and environment determine each other; most behavior is learned and adults are not victims of childhood.
He assessed behavior and cognitive variables through observation, self-reports and physiological measures, using controlled experiments and statistics.
Research links self-efficacy to age, gender, appearance, parenting, culture, school and job performance, physical and mental health and coping with stress.
Groups develop collective efficacy, which improves team, school, family, neighborhood and organizational outcomes; Internet self-efficacy shapes online behavior.
Exposure to violence on television, online and in video games increases aggression; disinhibition and unmonitored computer use feed cyberbullying.
Critics say the theory ignores emotion and inner causes and is vague about cognition, but it is objective, well supported, practical and used worldwide through media role models.
